source_anchors.exact_claim_quote:
At a fixed one-dimensional interior point, suppose the design density is
positive and $C^2$ locally, the chosen regression function is $C^2$ locally,
and the conditional response variance is finite and continuous. Suppose
$K$ is nonnegative, symmetric, positive near zero, normalized, with finite
positive second moment and finite squared integral. If $h_n\to0$,
$nh_n\to\infty$ and $nh_n^3\to\infty$, then the empirical local-linear fit
with a fixed fallback only on singular designs has a Lebesgue expectation
(and hence an unconditional second-order mean-bias expansion).

source_anchors.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix $n\ge1$, a point
$x\in\mathbb R$, bandwidth $h>0$, degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K$, and fallback $a_0\in\mathbb R$. Set
$u_i=(x-X_i)/h$, $r_p(u)=(1,u,\ldots,u^p)^\mathsf T$, let $Z$ be the matrix
whose $i$th row is $r_p(u_i)^\mathsf T$, let
$W=\operatorname{diag}(K(u_1),\ldots,K(u_n))$, and put
$M=Z^\mathsf TWZ$. If $M$ is nonsingular, define
$$\widehat\beta=M^{-1}Z^\mathsf TW(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^\mathsf T,\qquad \widehat m_{p,h}(x)=\widehat\beta_0.$$
If $M$ is singular, define $\widehat m_{p,h}(x)=a_0$. For fixed $x,h,n,p$
and Borel $K$, this is a real statistic estimating the pointwise target
$m(x)$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The case $p=1$ is the
**local-linear estimator**. No claim that $M$ is nonsingular for a given
sample is implicit in this definition.

source_anchors.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$,
a prediction point $x\in\mathbb R$, a bandwidth $h>0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$, and a fixed fallback
$a_0\in\mathbb R$. For data $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$, put
$$D_{n,h}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h).$$
The **Nadaraya–Watson estimator** of the pointwise target $m(x)$ is
$$\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h}(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h)Y_i}{D_{n,h}(x)},&D_{n,h}(x)>0,\\[6pt] a_0,&D_{n,h}(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
For fixed $x,h,n$, this is a statistic of the observed sample with real target
$m(x)$, in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The fallback is part
of the definition. Kernel regularity and bandwidth assumptions used for bias
or variance results are stated in those results.

source_anchors.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC as used to select the regression version. Fix a statistical experiment indexed by $\theta$, a point $x$, a real
regression target $m_\theta(x)$, and a real-valued estimator
$T_x$ of that target, meaning a measurable statistic with target space
$\mathbb R$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. At this point, use the
squared-error loss
$$L_x(\theta,a)=(a-m_\theta(x))^2,\qquad a\in\mathbb R.$$
Its **pointwise squared-error risk** is the possibly infinite quantity
$$R_x(\theta,T_x)=\int (T_x(z)-m_\theta(x))^2\,P_\theta(dz)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the deterministic-rule specialization of the risk in
[[def-loss-function-and-risk]]: the action space is $\mathbb R$ with its
Borel sigma-algebra, the action is $T_x(z)$, and the loss section is
measurable because it is continuous in $a$. The integral is nonnegative, so
it is defined without a finite-moment assumption.

source_anchors.exact_claim_quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real random variables on a probability
space, with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, and choose a regular conditional law
$Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$. On
$D=\{x:\int |y|\,Q(x,dy)<\infty\}$ define
$m(x)=\int y\,Q(x,dy)$, and put $m(x)=0$ off $D$. By
[[cor-conditional-expectation-as-a-measurable-function-of-the-conditioning-variable]],
$m$ is Borel measurable and $m(X)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(X)]$. A **regression target** is the resulting
$P_X$-almost-sure equivalence class; a **chosen regression-function version**
is the particular Borel function selected by the specified conditional law.

Pointwise smoothness is an additional hypothesis on the chosen version. It is
not implied by existence of conditional expectation, and statements about
$m(x)$ at a specified point use that selected version.

source_anchors.exact_claim_quote:
Let $X_i$ be iid real random variables with density $f$ continuous and
positive at a fixed point $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative,
symmetric, with $\int K=1$ and $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, a globally bounded density $f$, or a bounded
rapid-tail kernel satisfying $\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$.
For $h=h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, set $U_i=(x-X_i)/h_n$ and
$$M_n=\frac1{nh_n}\sum_{i=1}^nK(U_i)\begin{pmatrix}1\\U_i\end{pmatrix}(1,U_i).$$
Then
$$M_n\longrightarrow f(x)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu_2\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{in probability},$$
and $\mathbb P(M_n\text{ is nonsingular})\to1$.
More generally, the proof establishes $(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_i L(U_i)\to f(x)\int L$
for any integrable Borel function $L$, if $f$ is bounded globally or $L$
has compact support. Boundedness or square integrability of $L$ is unnecessary.

source_anchors.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC for the chosen regression version. Let $X_i$ be independent and
identically distributed with density $f$ continuous and positive at an
interior point $x$. For the chosen conditional law $Q(t,dy)$ in
[[def-regression-target-version]], set
$\sigma^2(t)=\int (y-m(t))^2Q(t,dy)$ where finite. Conditional on the
predictor vector, assume the responses are independent, have means $m(X_i)$,
and have variances $\sigma^2(X_i)$, where $\sigma^2$ is finite and continuous
at $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative, symmetric, with $\int K=1$,
$0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$ and $R(K)=\int K^2<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, globally bounded $f,\sigma^2$, or the
rapid-tail alternative: $\mathbb E Y^2<\infty$, bounded $K$, and
$\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$. In this last alternative the stated
local continuity is sufficient.
For the local-linear conclusion also assume $\int u^2K(u)^2\,du<\infty$;
this extra squared moment is automatic for compactly supported kernels.
The Nadaraya–Watson conclusion requires only $R(K)<\infty$. For $h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, use the fixed
fallbacks in [[def-nadaraya-watson-estimator]] and
[[def-local-polynomial-estimator]]. Then, with variance taken conditionally
on $X_1,\ldots,X_n$,
$$nh_n\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x)\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n) \longrightarrow \frac{R(K)\sigma^2(x)}{f(x)} \quad\text{in probability},$$
and the same limit holds with $\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x)$ replaced by
the degree-one local-linear estimator. This is a conditional-variance
statement for both estimators. If additionally $m$ is continuous at $x$
and bounded globally (only bounded near $x$ is required for compact $K$),
or if the rapid-tail alternative holds and $m$ is continuous at $x$,
with $nh_n^3\to\infty$ additionally in this rapid-tail unconditional clause,
then the Nadaraya–Watson estimator is square-integrable for large $n$ and
$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x))=\frac{R(K)\sigma^2(x)}{nh_nf(x)}+o((nh_n)^{-1}).$$
No unconditional local-linear variance is asserted: near-singular designs
can make even its finite-sample expectation undefined.

source_anchors.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC for the chosen regression version [[def-regression-target-version]].
Let $X$ have Lebesgue density $f$, with $f(x)>0$ at a fixed interior point
$x$, and let $f,m$ be $C^2$ near $x$. Let $K$ be a finite-valued Borel,
nonnegative, symmetric kernel with $\int K=1$,
$0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$ and $\int K^2<\infty$.
Assume either that $K$ has compact support, or that $f,m$ and their first
two derivatives are bounded and continuous on $\mathbb R$. In these first two alternatives, no continuity
or boundedness of $K$ is required. The global alternative supplies tail
control for noncompact kernels; local smoothness alone does not supply it.
A further localization alternative, including the Gaussian kernel, is that
$\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$, $K$ is bounded, and
$$\lim_{A\to\infty}\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)=0.$$
Under this rapid-tail alternative only the stated local smoothness of
$f,m$ is needed; no global boundedness of $m$ or of its derivatives is assumed.
For sufficiently small $h>0$, the population smoother corresponding to
[[def-nadaraya-watson-estimator]] is well defined by
$$m_h(x)=\frac{\int K(u)m(x-hu)f(x-hu)\,du}{\int K(u)f(x-hu)\,du},$$
and
$$m_h(x)-m(x)=\frac{h^2\mu_2}{2}\left(m''(x)+2m'(x)\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\right)+o(h^2).$$

## Definition

Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval and let $a\le t_1<\cdots<t_r\le b$ with $r\ge2$. A natural cubic spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is a $C^2$ function on $[a,b]$ that is a polynomial of degree at most three on every $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, has second derivative zero at $t_1$ and $t_r$, and is extended linearly on $[a,t_1]$ and $[t_r,b]$ when those intervals are nonempty. The knots $t_j$ are the distinct breakpoints; repeated observations at the same input do not create additional knots.

## Definition

Fix a degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$, an exponent $1\le q\le\infty$, and an integer $0\le l\le p$. A **local quasi-interpolant** is a linear map $Q$ from continuous $L^q$ functions on $[a,b]$ into $S_{p,\xi}$ with the following properties. For every nonempty knot interval $I_m$, there is a neighborhood $J_m\subseteq[a,b]$ that is a union of at most $M$ adjacent knot intervals such that (i) if $f=g$ almost everywhere on $J_m$, then $Qf=Qg$ almost everywhere on $I_m$; (ii) $Qv=v$ for every $v\in\mathcal P_l$; and (iii) for a constant $C_Q$ independent of the mesh, $\|Qf\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le C_Q\|f\|_{L^q(J_m)}$. Here $M$ bounds both the number of intervals in each $J_m$ and the number of neighborhoods $J_m$ containing any one point. The derivative and continuous-representative conventions for Sobolev inputs are those of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[cor-one-dimensional-w-one-p-functions-have-absolutely-continuous-representatives]].

The coefficient-functional formulation in Lyche–Manni–Speleers is one sufficient way to obtain these local stability and reproduction properties. The definition here records the operator hypotheses used in the approximation proof.

## Statement

Let $r\ge2$, $a\le x_1<\cdots<x_r\le b$, and $y_1,\ldots,y_r\in\mathbb R$. There is exactly one natural cubic spline $s$ on $[a,b]$ with $s(x_i)=y_i$ for each $i$. On each interval $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ it is the cubic with endpoint values $y_i,y_{i+1}$ and endpoint second derivatives $M_i,M_{i+1}$, where $M_1=M_r=0$ and the interior values solve the positive-definite tridiagonal system
$$h_{i-1}M_{i-1}+2(h_{i-1}+h_i)M_i+h_iM_{i+1}=6\left(\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{h_i}-\frac{y_i-y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\right),\quad 2\le i\le r-1,$$
with $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$. The interpolant is linear outside $[x_1,x_r]$.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 Put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$. For $r=2$ there are no interior second derivatives to solve. For $r\ge3$, let $A$ be the $(r-2)\times(r-2)$ symmetric tridiagonal matrix with diagonal entry $2(h_{i-1}+h_i)$ in row $i$ and adjacent off-diagonal entries $h_i$. For a nonzero vector $v=(v_2,\ldots,v_{r-1})$, using $2v_iv_{i+1}\ge-v_i^2-v_{i+1}^2$ gives $v^TAv\ge\sum_{i=2}^{r-1}(h_{i-1}+h_i)v_i^2>0.$ Thus $A$ is positive definite and invertible, so the displayed system has exactly one solution $M_2,\ldots,M_{r-1}$. [A1, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 3.1 Any natural cubic interpolant has nodal second derivatives with $M_1=M_r=0$. Equality of its adjacent endpoint slopes forces the displayed tridiagonal equations, so by step 1.1 its nodal second derivatives equal the constructed ones. On each interval, the difference from $s_i$ is a cubic with zero second derivative at both endpoints; its second derivative is affine and therefore zero throughout, so the difference is affine and vanishes at both endpoint values. It is identically zero. Thus the interpolant is unique. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $p_K(x)=(B_{1,p,\xi}(x),\ldots,B_{K,p,\xi}(x))^T$ be a specified degree-$p$ B-spline basis on the data domain, and let $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be observed real-valued data. Form the design matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times K}$ with row $p_K(X_i)^T$. The **series least-squares fitted training vector** is
$$\widehat{\mathbf g}_K=\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(P)}\mathbf Y,$$
the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^T$ onto the column space of $P$. Conditional on the realized design, this is the fixed-design least-squares fitted vector of [[def-fixed-design-projection-estimator]]. Equivalently, it is $P\widehat\beta$ for any minimizer $\widehat\beta$ of $\|\mathbf Y-P\beta\|_2^2$; all such minimizers have the same fitted training vector. The training prediction loss relative to a specified target vector $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$ is $n^{-1}\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2$. This definition specifies training fitted values and makes no test-risk assertion.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p\ge0$, $0\le l\le p$, $1\le q\le\infty$, and let $Q$ be a bounded local quasi-interpolant as in [[def-local-spline-quasi-interpolant]] on a knot mesh in $[a,b]$. Let $f\in W^{l+1,q}(a,b)$ and use its continuous Sobolev representative. For each nonempty mesh cell $I_m$, let $J_m$ be the corresponding neighborhood, let $h_m$ be the largest cell length in $J_m$, and suppose $|J_m|\le M h_m$ with overlap multiplicity at most $M$. Then
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q(I_m)}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1}}{l!}h_m^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J_m)}.$$
Writing $h=\max_m h_m$, the global bound is
$$\|f-Qf\|_{L^q([a,b])}\le (1+C_Q)\frac{M^{l+1+1/q}}{l!}h^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q([a,b])},$$
where $1/q=0$ for $q=\infty$. In particular, on a uniform mesh with interior knots of multiplicity $p+1$, the cellwise $L^2$ projector onto $\mathcal P_p$ is a local quasi-interpolant and gives the order-$h^s$ approximation bound for every integer $1\le s\le p+1$.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 On any neighborhood $J=[c,d]$, use the continuous representatives of $D^jf$, $0\le j\le l$, supplied by [F2]. Their Sobolev-class convention [F1] and the choice hypotheses for [F2] are available under [A1] by [F5]. Repeated integration by parts for absolutely continuous functions gives the Taylor identity $f(x)-T_{c,l}f(x)=\frac1{l!}\int_c^x(x-t)^lD^{l+1}f(t)\,dt,$ where $T_{c,l}f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^lD^jf(c)(x-c)^j/j!$. For completeness, the case $l=0$ is the increment formula in [F2]; passing from order $l-1$ to $l$ integrates $\int_c^x(x-t)^{l-1}D^lf(t)dt$ by parts with antiderivative $-(x-t)^l/l$, producing the degree-$l$ endpoint term and the displayed remainder. Hölder [F3] therefore gives $\|f-T_{c,l}f\|_{L^q(J)}\le |J|^{l+1}\|D^{l+1}f\|_{L^q(J)}/l!$, including $q=\infty$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F5, given, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 4.1 For a uniform mesh with interior knots repeated $p+1$ times, $S_{p,\xi}$ is the space of independent degree-$p$ polynomials on the cells by the definition and basis theorem. Define $Q_hf$ on each cell as the orthogonal projection of $f$ onto $\mathcal P_p$. By [F4] it is linear and contractive in $L^2$; it depends only on that cell, takes values in $S_{p,\xi}$, and fixes every member of $\mathcal P_p$. Thus it satisfies the local quasi-interpolant hypotheses with one-cell neighborhoods, $M=1$, and $C_Q=1$. ## Statement

Let $n,K\ge1$, let $X_i\in[a,b]$ and $Y_i\in\mathbb R$ be iid pairs, and suppose the one-observation law is $P_X(dx)\kappa(x,dy)$ for a supplied Borel probability kernel $\kappa$ from $([a,b],\mathcal B([a,b]))$ to $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$. Assume a Borel function $g_0:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is supplied such that, for $P_X$-almost every $x$, $\int |y|\,\kappa(x,dy)<\infty$, $g_0(x)=\int y\,\kappa(x,dy)$, and $\int (y-g_0(x))^2\,\kappa(x,dy)\le\Delta$ for a finite $\Delta\ge0$. Let $p_K:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^K$ be a fixed Borel $K$-dimensional spline basis and assume a deterministic $\bar\beta_K\in\mathbb R^K$ and constants $C,\gamma>0$ satisfy
$$E\{g_0(X)-p_K(X)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\le C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
Then, with the fitted training vector $\widehat{\mathbf g}_K$ from [[def-series-spline-least-squares]] and $\mathbf g_0=(g_0(X_1),\ldots,g_0(X_n))^T$,
$$E\left[\frac1n\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g_0\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\Delta K}{n}+C^2K^{-2\gamma}.$$
This is expected empirical training-design loss.

For fixed $\mathbf x$, set $\kappa_1=\kappa(x_1,\cdot)$ and, for $1\le m<n$, apply [F10] to $\kappa_m$ and $\kappa(x_{m+1},\cdot)$ to obtain $\kappa_{m+1}$; both factors are probability measures, so the rectangle formula gives total mass one at each stage. Induction gives the finite product probability measure $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ with rectangle values $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\prod_iB_i)=\prod_i\kappa(x_i,B_i)$. The response rectangles form a pi-system because intersections of rectangles are rectangles, and [F5] says they generate the response product sigma-algebra. On response rectangles the evaluation is Borel in $\mathbf x$ by [F4] and [F10]. Because $\kappa_n(\mathbf x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, the class of sets with Borel evaluation contains the whole space, is closed under complements by subtraction from $1$, and is closed under disjoint countable unions by limits of partial sums; [F11] therefore gives measurability for every response Borel set. For rectangles $A=\prod_iA_i$ and $B=\prod_iB_i$, iid sampling gives $P(\mathbf X\in A,\mathbf Y\in B)=\prod_i\int_{A_i}\kappa(x,B_i)P_X(dx)$, and repeated Tonelli [F13] gives $\int_A\kappa_n(\mathbf x,B)P_X^{\otimes n}(d\mathbf x)=\prod_i\int_{A_i}\kappa(x,B_i)P_X(dx).$ For fixed response Borel $B$, the left side of the target identity is a finite measure in $A$; the right side is also a measure by [F12], applied to the nonnegative measurable function $\mathbf x\mapsto\kappa_n(\mathbf x,B)$. Design rectangles form a pi-system because intersections are rectangles and generate the design product sigma-algebra by [F5], so [F11] extends the equality to every design Borel $A$. Thus the response sets $B$ for which the identity holds for every $A$ form a Dynkin system (complements use the common total mass); they contain the response rectangles, so [F11] gives equality for every response Borel set. Hence $\kappa_n$ is a conditional law of $\mathbf Y$ given $\mathbf X$. Under this product law the residuals are conditionally independent, have conditional means zero by [A2], and conditional second moments at most $\Delta$. Hence $E[\epsilon_i\epsilon_j\mid\mathbf X]=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $E[\epsilon_i^2\mid\mathbf X]\le\Delta$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F4, F5, F10, F11, F12, F13, given, algebra, construct]

4.1 Taking expectations in step 3.1, applying step 2.1 and then iid sampling with [A3] yields $E\|\widehat{\mathbf g}_K-\mathbf g\|_2^2\le\Delta K+E\sum_{i=1}^n\{g_0(X_i)-p_K(X_i)^T\bar\beta_K\}^2\le\Delta K+nC^2K^{-2\gamma}.$ Divide by $n$ to obtain the claimed expected empirical training-risk bound. [A3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_J=1$ be a uniform partition with mesh $h=1/J$. For $f\in W^{2,\infty}(0,1)$, its continuous representative has a piecewise-linear interpolant $I_hf$ in the degree-one spline space with simple interior knots.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 On each cell $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, $I_hf(x)=\frac{t_{j+1}-x}{h}f(t_j)+\frac{x-t_j}{h}f(t_{j+1})$. The nonnegative weights sum to one, so $\|I_hf\|_{L^\infty([t_j,t_{j+1}])}\le\|f\|_{L^\infty([t_j,t_{j+1}])}$. It depends only on that cell, reproduces every affine function, and is a continuous piecewise-linear spline by [F1]. Thus it satisfies the hypotheses in [F2] with one-cell neighborhoods and $C_Q=1$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 2.1 Let $M_2=\|D^2f\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}$. On a cell $[u,v]$ of length $h$, put $a_x=x-u$ and $b_x=v-x$. By [F3] applied to $f$ and $Df$, let $f^*$ and $g^*$ be their absolutely continuous representatives; $(g^*)'=D^2f$ almost everywhere and $f^*(x)-f^*(u)=\int_u^xg^*(s)\,ds$. The absolutely continuous function $t\mapsto(x-t)g^*(t)$ has derivative $-g^*(t)+(x-t)D^2f(t)$ almost everywhere, so the fundamental theorem for absolutely continuous functions gives $f^*(x)=f^*(u)+a_xg^*(u)+\int_u^x(x-t)D^2f(t)\,dt$, and the same formula at $v$. Since $I_hf(x)=f^*(u)+(a_x/h)(f^*(v)-f^*(u))$, subtraction and simplification yield $f^*(x)-I_hf(x)=-\int_u^x\frac{b_x(t-u)}hD^2f(t)\,dt-\int_x^v\frac{a_x(v-t)}hD^2f(t)\,dt$. Hence $|f^*(x)-I_hf(x)|\le M_2\{b_xa_x^2/(2h)+a_xb_x^2/(2h)\}=M_2a_xb_x/2\le M_2h^2/8$, since $a_x+b_x=h$ and $a_xb_x\le h^2/4$. This holds on every cell and at every point, so taking the supremum gives $\|f-I_hf\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}\le h^2\|D^2f\|_{L^\infty(0,1)}/8$. [A2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Use the degree-one clamped B-spline basis $p(x)=(1-x,x)$ on $[0,1]$, with a single fixed training input $x_1=1/2$ and response $y_1=1$. The coefficient vector $\widehat\beta=(0,2)^T$ is a least-squares minimizer and gives the fitted function $\widehat g(x)=2x$. Let the target be $g_0(x)=1$ and the independent test input be uniform on $[0,1]$.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 On the clamped knot vector $(0,0,1,1)$, the only nonzero degree-zero spline on $(0,1)$ is $B_{2,0}=1$; the recurrence in [F3] gives $B_{1,1}=1-x$ and $B_{2,1}=x$, so $p(1/2)=(1/2,1/2)$. Therefore $p(1/2)^T\widehat\beta=(1/2,1/2)(0,2)^T=1$, the training residual and empirical training loss are zero, and the fitted vector equals the projection in [F1]. The chosen coefficient vector is one admissible representation of it. [A1, F1, F3, given, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 2.1 The independent test squared error has expectation $E\{\widehat g(X')-g_0(X')\}^2=\int_0^1(2x-1)^2dx=\frac43-2+1=\frac13>0.$ Thus zero training loss does not imply zero independent test loss, consistent with the scope of [F2]. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable, symmetric and quasi-convex, with $M>0$. For integers $N\ge2$ and $m\ge1$, put $\delta=M/N$, $C_k=\overline{\{x:L(x)\le k\delta\}}$ and
$$g_{N,m}(x)=\delta\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\min(1,m\,d(x,C_k)).$$
For $C_k=\varnothing$ the corresponding summand is defined to be one, and for $C_k=\mathbb R^d$ it is zero. Then $0\le g_{N,m}\le L$, and $g_{N,m}$ is bounded and Lipschitz. For every nondegenerate Gaussian $H\sim N_d(b,S)$,
$$\inf_a E g_{N,m}(a-H)=E g_{N,m}(H-b),\qquad \lim_{N\to\infty}\lim_{m\to\infty}E g_{N,m}(H-b)=E L(H-b).$$
Each summand is symmetric and quasi-convex; no quasi-convexity of their sum is asserted.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 Each sublevel $A_k=\{L\le k\delta\}$ is convex and symmetric by hypothesis. Its closure $C_k$ is closed; it is convex by [F10] when $A_k$ is nonempty, and is convex by vacuity when $A_k=\varnothing$. If $x\in C_k$, [F11] supplies $x_j\in A_k$ with $x_j\to x$; then $-x_j\in A_k$ and $-x\in C_k$, so $C_k$ is symmetric (the empty case is symmetric as well). For a nonempty closed convex $C$, choose $c_x,c_y\in C$ within $\epsilon$ of $d(x,C),d(y,C)$ using [F6]. Their convex combination lies in $C$, and [F7] gives $d((1-t)x+ty,C)\le(1-t)d(x,C)+td(y,C)+\epsilon$. Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ to prove convexity of the distance function. When $C=-C$, replacing each $c$ by $-c$ in the infimum shows $d(-x,C)=d(x,C)$. Thus for a nonempty proper $C_k$, $q(x)=\min(1,m d(x,C_k))$ is symmetric; its sublevel at $0\le t<1$ is $\{d(x,C_k)\le t/m\}$, which is convex, and its sublevel for $t\ge1$ is the whole space. It is Borel and $m$-Lipschitz by [F1] and [F9]. For empty $C_k$ or $C_k=\mathbb R^d$, the stated constant conventions have the same properties. [A1, F1, F6, F7, F9, F10, F11, given, choose, construct, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 3.1 Since $C_k$ is closed, its $k$th term increases to $\mathbf1_{C_k^c}$ as $m\to\infty$. If $C_k=\mathbb R^d$, then [F10] gives $\operatorname{int}\{L\le k\delta\}=\mathbb R^d$, so the level set is all of $\mathbb R^d$ and both indicators vanish. If $C_k=\varnothing$, the level set is empty and both indicators equal one. Otherwise the difference between $\{L>k\delta\}$ and $C_k^c$ is contained in the boundary of the convex set $\{L\le k\delta\}$, which is null by [F2]. By [F4], it is null under the centered Gaussian as well. Therefore F5 gives $\lim_m E g_{N,m}(H-b)=E[\delta\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\mathbf1_{\{L(H-b)>k\delta\}}]$. The expression inside the expectation differs from $L(H-b)$ by at most $\delta$: count the grid thresholds strictly below each value in $[0,M]$. Let $N\to\infty$ to obtain the second identity. [A1, F2, F4, F5, F9, F10, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and [[def-qmd-path]] at $\theta_0$ with score $s$ and information $I$.
Let $h_n\to h$ in $\mathbb R^d$, put $u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$, and write
$P_0=P_{\theta_0}$ and $P_{u_n}=P_{\theta_0+u_n}$. On
$S=\{p_{\theta_0}>0\}$ define, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$q_n(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_S(x)p_{\theta_0+u_n}(x)} {(1-\alpha_n)p_{\theta_0}(x)},\qquad \alpha_n=P_{u_n}(S^c).$$
Then $q_n$ is a probability density relative to $P_0$. For IID
$X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, let $L_n=\prod_{i=1}^nq_n(X_i)$ and
$\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$. Under $P_0^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad P_0^{\otimes n}(L_n=0)\to0.$$
Moreover, if $\bar P_n=q_nP_0$ is the normalized absolutely continuous
component of $P_{u_n}$ relative to $P_0$, then
$$\|P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}-\bar P_n^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}\to0.$$
No full likelihood ratio for $P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}$ is asserted.

Define $q_u=\mathbf1_Sp_u/((1-\alpha(u))p_0)$ on $S$ and $q_u=0$ on $S^c$. It is nonnegative and measurable, and $\int q_u\,dP_0=(1-\alpha(u))^{-1}\int_Sp_u\,d\mu=1,$ so it is a probability density. At $u=0$, $\alpha(0)=0$ and $q_0=1$ $P_0$-almost surely, since $P_0(S^c)=\int_{S^c}p_0\,d\mu=0$. On $S$, $\sqrt{q_u}=(1-\alpha(u))^{-1/2} \left(1+\tfrac12u^Ts+\frac{r_u}{\sqrt{p_0}}\right).$ The residual term has $L^2(P_0)$ norm $\|r_u\mathbf1_S\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(\|u\|_2)$. Also $|(1-\alpha)^{-1/2}-1| =\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{1-\alpha}(1+\sqrt{1-\alpha})}=O(\alpha),$ and [F2], [F8] give $\|u^Ts\|_{L^2(P_0)}=O(\|u\|_2)$. Therefore $Y_u:=2(\sqrt{q_u}-1)=u^Ts+R_u, \qquad\|R_u\|_{L^2(P_0)}=o(\|u\|_2).$ This is the required square-root expansion. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F8, L1, given, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 5.1 The full one-observation law decomposes as $P_{u_n}=(1-\alpha_n)\bar P_n+\alpha_n S_n$, where $S_n$ is the normalized restriction of $P_{u_n}$ to $S^c$ when $\alpha_n>0$. In the product mixture, the probability that at least one coordinate is drawn from $S_n$ is at most $n\alpha_n$. Conditioning on the all-absolutely-continuous component shows, for every event, its probability under the full product differs from that under $\bar P_n^{\otimes n}$ by at most $n\alpha_n$. Since $n\alpha_n=o(n\|u_n\|_2^2)=o(1)$, [F7] proves the total-variation claim. If $\alpha_n=0$, the singular component is absent and the same bound is zero. [F3, F7, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and [[def-qmd-path]] at $\theta_0$ with score $s$ and information $I$.
Let $h_n\to h$ in $\mathbb R^d$, put $u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$, and write
$P_0=P_{\theta_0}$ and $P_{u_n}=P_{\theta_0+u_n}$. On
$S=\{p_{\theta_0}>0\}$ define, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$q_n(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_S(x)p_{\theta_0+u_n}(x)} {(1-\alpha_n)p_{\theta_0}(x)},\qquad \alpha_n=P_{u_n}(S^c).$$
Then $q_n$ is a probability density relative to $P_0$. For IID
$X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, let $L_n=\prod_{i=1}^nq_n(X_i)$ and
$\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$. Under $P_0^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad P_0^{\otimes n}(L_n=0)\to0.$$
Moreover, if $\bar P_n=q_nP_0$ is the normalized absolutely continuous
component of $P_{u_n}$ relative to $P_0$, then
$$\|P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}-\bar P_n^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}\to0.$$
No full likelihood ratio for $P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}$ is asserted.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 Write $p_u=p_{\theta_0+u}$, $S=\{p_0>0\}$, and $\alpha(u)=\int_{S^c}p_u\,d\mu$. For small $u$, [F3] gives $\alpha(u)<1/2$. Define $q_u=\mathbf1_Sp_u/((1-\alpha(u))p_0)$ on $S$ and $q_u=0$ on $S^c$. It is nonnegative and measurable, and $\int q_u\,dP_0=(1-\alpha(u))^{-1}\int_Sp_u\,d\mu=1,$ so it is a probability density. At $u=0$, $\alpha(0)=0$ and $q_0=1$ $P_0$-almost surely, since $P_0(S^c)=\int_{S^c}p_0\,d\mu=0$. On $S$, $\sqrt{q_u}=(1-\alpha(u))^{-1/2} \left(1+\tfrac12u^Ts+\frac{r_u}{\sqrt{p_0}}\right).$ The residual term has $L^2(P_0)$ norm $\|r_u\mathbf1_S\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(\|u\|_2)$. Also $|(1-\alpha)^{-1/2}-1| =\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{1-\alpha}(1+\sqrt{1-\alpha})}=O(\alpha),$ and [F2], [F8] give $\|u^Ts\|_{L^2(P_0)}=O(\|u\|_2)$. Therefore $Y_u:=2(\sqrt{q_u}-1)=u^Ts+R_u, \qquad\|R_u\|_{L^2(P_0)}=o(\|u\|_2).$ This is the required square-root expansion. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F8, L1, given, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 5.1 The full one-observation law decomposes as $P_{u_n}=(1-\alpha_n)\bar P_n+\alpha_n S_n$, where $S_n$ is the normalized restriction of $P_{u_n}$ to $S^c$ when $\alpha_n>0$. In the product mixture, the probability that at least one coordinate is drawn from $S_n$ is at most $n\alpha_n$. Conditioning on the all-absolutely-continuous component shows, for every event, its probability under the full product differs from that under $\bar P_n^{\otimes n}$ by at most $n\alpha_n$. Since $n\alpha_n=o(n\|u_n\|_2^2)=o(1)$, [F7] proves the total-variation claim. If $\alpha_n=0$, the singular component is absent and the same bound is zero. [F3, F7, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subseteq
\mathbb R^d\}$ be dominated by a common sigma-finite measure, with $\Theta$
open, and suppose the model is QMD at an interior $\theta_0$ with score $s$
and information $I=E_{\theta_0}[ss^T]$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID
$P_{\theta_0}$, and for each fixed local sequence $h_n\to h$ set
$u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$. Then the local product laws
$P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}$ admit mean-one likelihood-ratio proxies
$L_n$ relative to $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$ such that
$$\left\|P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV} \to0,$$
and under $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)\Rightarrow N_d(0,I).$$
Thus the IID QMD experiment is LAN in the proxy sense of
[[def-lan-experiment]]. This assertion does not claim that the full local
product law has a Radon–Nikodym derivative relative to the base law.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 By [A1, L1, F1] the path is QMD with the specified density versions. [F2] applies to the chosen sequence $u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$ and supplies the normalized proxy $L_n$, the total variation approximation, and the log expansion. Its normalizer is $1-\alpha_n>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, since $\alpha_n=o(\|u_n\|_2^2)$ and $u_n\to0$. [A1, F1, F2, L1, given]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 2.1 For each fixed $h$, steps 1.1 and 1.2 give the proxy approximation, the log expansion and the Gaussian central-sequence limit required in [F4]. Hence the local experiment is LAN. The proof used the full likelihood only for the normalized absolutely continuous component; singular mass is handled by the total-variation bound in [F2]. This proves the stated proxy-LAN conclusion. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID $N(\theta,1)$ and take $\theta_0=0$. This
one-dimensional model is QMD at zero with score $s(x)=x$ and information
$I=1$. For every fixed $h$, the local laws $P_{n,h}=N(h/\sqrt n,1)^{\otimes n}$
are exactly dominated by $P_{n,0}$ and
$$\log\frac{dP_{n,h}}{dP_{n,0}}(X_1,\ldots,X_n) =h\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^2,\qquad \Delta_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
The sample mean estimator is regular, with
$$\sqrt n\left(\bar X_n-\frac h{\sqrt n}\right)\Rightarrow N(0,1)$$
under $P_{n,h}$ for each fixed $h$.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 Let $g_\theta(x)=\sqrt{\phi(x-\theta)} =(2\pi)^{-1/4}e^{-(x-\theta)^2/4}$. By [F6] its derivative is $\partial_\theta g_\theta(x)=\tfrac12(x-\theta)g_\theta(x)$, so $\partial_\theta g_0(x)=\tfrac12xg_0(x)$. For $|\theta|\le1$, $|\partial_\theta g_\theta(x)| \le C(1+|x|)e^{-((|x|-1)_+)^2/4}=:G(x),$ whose square is integrable: it is bounded on $[-2,2]$, and for $|x|\ge2$ it is bounded by $C'(1+x^2)e^{-x^2/8}$. Substituting $x=2y$ reduces the tail integral to a constant times $\int(1+4y^2)e^{-y^2/2}dy$, finite by the second moment statement in [F2]. By [F7], $(g_t-g_0)/t=\int_0^1\partial_\theta g_{rt}\,dr$; this converges pointwise to $\tfrac12xg_0$. Its difference is bounded by $2G$, so [F5] applied to the squared difference gives convergence in $L^2(dx)$. Thus the QMD residual has norm $o(|t|)$, which is exactly the scalar QMD condition. [F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, F11, given, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 3.1 Under $P_{n,h}$, the variables $X_i-h/\sqrt n$ are IID $N(0,1)$. The same characteristic-function product using [F3]–[F4] gives $\sqrt n\left(\bar X_n-\frac h{\sqrt n}\right) =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_i(X_i-h/\sqrt n)\sim N(0,1)$ exactly, which implies the displayed convergence. The limiting law does not depend on fixed $h$, which is regularity by [F9]. The calculation includes $h=0$ and every finite $h$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F9, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID from a probability law $P$ that is misspecified relative to the density family $p_\theta$, and let $\ell_\theta=\log p_\theta$ be as in [[def-pseudo-true-parameter-under-misspecification]]. Write $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nf(X_i)$ and $M(\theta)=\mathbb E_P\ell_\theta(X)$. Assume that $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and that $\theta^*$ is the unique separated interior maximizer of $M$, where interior means that some Euclidean open ball about $\theta^*$ lies in $\Theta$: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\eta_\varepsilon>0$ such that $M(\theta^*)-M(\theta)\ge\eta_\varepsilon$ whenever $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\ge\varepsilon$. Assume the uniform law $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|\to_P0$, and let $\hat\theta_n\in\Theta$ be a measurable approximate maximizer with $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\ell_\theta-P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}\to_P0$.

Let $S_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x)$ be continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $\theta^*$. Assume $\mathbb E_PS_{\theta^*}=0$, $\mathbb E_P\|S_{\theta^*}\|_2^2<\infty$, and set $J=\mathbb E_P[S_{\theta^*}S_{\theta^*}^{T}]$. Suppose $H=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_{\theta^*}]$ is nonsingular, $D(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\nabla_\theta S_\theta]$ exists and is continuous at $\theta^*$, and for every sufficiently small fixed $\delta>0$,

$$\sup_{\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\le\delta}\|P_n\nabla_\theta S_\theta-D(\theta)\|_{op}\to_P0,$$

where $\|A\|_{op}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2\le1}\|Av\|_2$. Finally assume the approximate score equation $\sqrt n\,P_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=o_P(1)$. Then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta^*)\Rightarrow N_d\!\left(0,H^{-1}JH^{-T}\right).$$

The covariance is the sandwich matrix formed from the Hessian $H$ under $P$ and the score second moment $J$ under $P$. The theorem does not assert that it equals the inverse Fisher information of the fitted model.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 Put $\Delta_n=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|P_n\ell_\theta-M(\theta)|$ and $r_n=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\ell_\theta-P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}$. By assumption $\Delta_n\to_P0$ and $r_n\to_P0$. Since $\hat\theta_n$ is an approximate maximizer by [F8], $P_n\ell_{\hat\theta_n}\ge P_n\ell_{\theta^*}-r_n$, and therefore $0\le M(\theta^*)-M(\hat\theta_n)\le2\Delta_n+r_n$. [given, F1, F3, F7, F8, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 5.1 By [F2], the score vectors $S_{\theta^*}(X_i)$ are IID; their mean is zero and their covariance is $J$. Their second moment is finite by the Statement, so [F4] and [A1] give $\sqrt nP_nS_{\theta^*}\Rightarrow G$ with $G\sim N_d(0,J)$. The matrix $A_n^{-1}$ converges in probability in operator norm to $H^{-1}$, and the residual vector $\sqrt nP_nS_{\hat\theta_n}=o_P(1)$ by the Statement. Flattening the matrix entries and concatenating the vectors gives a finite-dimensional vector converging in probability to $(H^{-1},0)$. Applying [F5] to the continuous map $(x,A,r)\mapsto-Ax+Ar$ gives the limit $-H^{-1}G$. Its covariance is $H^{-1}JH^{-T}$, proving the assertion. [A1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.

Inductively, each degree-$p$ term is a lower-degree spline multiplied by an affine factor; on the lower-degree spline's support that factor is nonnegative, and the two supports lie inside $[\xi_j, \xi_{j+p+1}]$. Thus support, degree at most $p$, and nonnegativity hold for every $p$. [A1, F1, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 4.1 The smoothness and piecewise-degree properties from steps 1.1 and 3.2 put every B-spline in $S_{p,\xi}$. If a linear combination of all $n$ B-splines is zero, then on every nonempty knot interval its active coefficients vanish by the local basis property in step 3.1. Each B-spline has a nonempty support interval by the clamped-knot hypothesis, so every coefficient occurs on at least one such interval and is zero. The B-splines are therefore $n$ independent members of the $n$-dimensional space in step 1.3, hence form its basis. The unique global expansion includes every polynomial from step 2.1. [A1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.3, step 1.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be one measurable space and let $P_n,Q_n$ be
probability measures on it ([[def-probability-measure]]). The sequence
$(Q_n)$ is **contiguous with respect to** $(P_n)$, written $Q_n\triangleleft
P_n$, if for every sequence $A_n\in\mathcal A$,
$$P_n(A_n)\longrightarrow0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q_n(A_n)\longrightarrow0.$$
The sequences are **mutually contiguous**, written $Q_n\triangleleft\triangleright
P_n$, if both $Q_n\triangleleft P_n$ and $P_n\triangleleft Q_n$.

Contiguity is a relation between sequences of laws, not absolute continuity at
each finite $n$. It says that events negligible under one sequence remain
negligible under the other in the indicated direction.

## Definition

Let $P_{n,h}$ be probability laws on a common measurable space for each
integer $n\ge1$ and local parameter $h\in\mathbb R^d$, where $d<\infty$ and
$P_{n,0}$ is the base law. Suppose that for every fixed $h$ we are supplied a
nonnegative measurable function $L_{n,h}$ with
$$\int L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}=1.$$
It defines an absolutely continuous proxy
$$\bar P_{n,h}(A):=\int_A L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}.$$
The actual local law is allowed to have a singular part; the approximation
condition below is what connects it to this proxy.

The experiments are **locally asymptotically normal (LAN)** at $h=0$ with
information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$ if $K$ is a symmetric
positive semidefinite $d\times d$ matrix, $\Delta_n$ is an $\mathbb R^d$-valued
statistic,
$$\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)\quad\text{under }P_{n,0},$$
and for every fixed $h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\|P_{n,h}-\bar P_{n,h}\|_{\rm TV}\to0,\qquad \log L_{n,h}=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TKh+o_{P_{n,0}}(1),$$
where $\|\cdot\|_{\rm TV}$ is the event-supremum total variation distance
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]) and
$o_{P_{n,0}}(1)$ means convergence to zero in $P_{n,0}$-probability. We set
$\log0=-\infty$; the finite-valued expansion entails
$P_{n,0}(L_{n,h}=0)\to0$. Convergence in distribution is as in
[[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], and $N_d(0,K)$ allows
singular $K$ ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

If $P_{n,h}=\bar P_{n,h}$, this is the usual dominated LAN comparison. The
proxy formulation also covers QMD paths whose local alternatives are not
absolutely continuous with respect to the base law, provided the singular
product mass tends to zero in total variation. This definition is pointwise
in each fixed $h$; it does not assert uniformity over bounded sets of $h$.

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be
nonempty compact convex sets. With $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}$ and
$\lambda_d$ denoting Lebesgue measure,
$$\lambda_d(A+B)^{1/d}\ge \lambda_d(A)^{1/d}+\lambda_d(B)^{1/d}.$$
Zero-volume and lower-dimensional sets are included.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 If one of $A,B$ has zero volume, say $\lambda_d(A)=0$, choose $a\in A$. By [F11], $A+B$ is compact and measurable. Then $a+B\subseteq A+B$, so [F6] gives $\lambda_d(A+B)\ge\lambda_d(B)$; the stated inequality follows after taking $d$th roots. If both volumes vanish the right side is zero. source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 8.1 The induction proves the normalized claim in every finite dimension. Undoing the normalization in step 2.1 gives $\lambda_d(A+B)^{1/d}\ge a+b =\lambda_d(A)^{1/d}+\lambda_d(B)^{1/d},$ including the zero-volume cases from step 1.1. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 7.1, algebra, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

For each $n$, let $P_n,Q_n$ be probability measures on one measurable space,
and let $L_n\ge0$ satisfy $Q_n(A)=\int_A L_n\,dP_n$ for every measurable
$A$. Suppose $E_{P_n}L_n=1$, $L_n\Rightarrow L$ under $P_n$, $L\ge0$, and
$E L=1$. Then $(Q_n)$ is contiguous with respect to $(P_n)$.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 For fixed $M>0$, $x\mapsto x\wedge M$ is bounded and continuous on $[0,\infty)$, so [F2] and the mean assumptions give $E(L_n-M)_+=E L_n-E(L_n\wedge M)\longrightarrow E L-E(L\wedge M)=E(L-M)_+.$ [F2, given, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 3.1 For any event sequence $A_n$ and any $M>0$, $Q_n(A_n)=E[L_n\mathbf1_{A_n}] \le M P_n(A_n)+E[L_n\mathbf1_{\{L_n>M\}}].$ If $P_n(A_n)\to0$, the first term tends to zero for fixed $M$, and uniform integrability makes the limsup of the second term arbitrarily small as $M\to\infty$. Thus $Q_n(A_n)\to0$, which is $Q_n\triangleleft P_n$ by [F1]. [F1, F2, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

In a local experiment $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ at $h=0$
([[def-lan-experiment]]), let $T_n$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued statistic.
It is **regular at zero with limit law $W$** if, for every fixed
$h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$T_n-h\Rightarrow W\quad\text{under }P_{n,h},$$
where the same probability law $W$ works for all $h$. In a parametric model
with true parameter $\theta_0$, this is the definition for
$T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ and local laws at
$\theta_0+h/\sqrt n$; equivalently the centered error
$\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0-h/\sqrt n)$ has a limit independent of
the fixed local displacement $h$.

## Statement

Assume AC.

Let $H\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact, let $\pi$ be a probability measure on
$H$, and let $P_{n,0}$ be base laws. Suppose $L_n(h,x)$ is jointly measurable
in $(h,x)$, nonnegative, and satisfies
$\int L_n(h,x)P_{n,0}(dx)=1$ for every $h\in H$. Let
$\Delta_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_d(0,K)$ under $P_{n,0}$, where $K$ is positive
semidefinite, and put
$$g_h(z)=\exp(h^Tz-\tfrac12h^TKh).$$
Assume the random variable
$$a_n(x):=\sup_{h\in H}|L_n(h,x)-g_h(\Delta_n(x))|$$
is measurable and $E_{P_{n,0}}a_n\to0$. Let the prior-predictive law be
$M_n(dx)=m_n(x)P_{n,0}(dx)$ with
$m_n(x)=\int_HL_n(h,x)\pi(dh)$, and define posteriors
$$\Pi_n(dh\mid x)=\frac{L_n(h,x)\pi(dh)}{m_n(x)},\qquad \Pi^G(dh\mid z)=\frac{g_h(z)\pi(dh)}{m(z)},\quad m(z)=\int_Hg_h(z)\pi(dh),$$
where an arbitrary probability measure is assigned if a denominator is zero.
Then
$$E_{M_n}\int_H\left| \frac{L_n(h,X)}{m_n(X)}- \frac{g_h(\Delta_n(X))}{m(\Delta_n(X))} \right|\pi(dh)\longrightarrow0.$$
In particular the posterior laws converge in expected total variation,
because their event-probability differences are bounded by this $L^1(\pi)$
distance. The convention for total variation is
[[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]].

This lemma assumes an $L^1$ uniform likelihood-field approximation. Pointwise
LAN alone does not supply that hypothesis.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 By [F4], integration against the prior makes $m_n$ measurable; [F6] gives $E_{P_{n,0}}m_n=1$. Also $|m_n(x)-m(\Delta_n(x))|\le a_n(x),$ so $E_{P_{n,0}}m(\Delta_n)\to1$. The function $m$ is continuous: if $z_j\to z$, then $g_h(z_j)\to g_h(z)$ for each $h$, and compactness of $H$ gives a common finite bound on $g_h(z_j)$; [F8] passes the limit through the prior integral. Thus [F1] and [F7] give $m(\Delta_n)\Rightarrow m(Z)$. By [F3], $E m(Z)=1$. Dividing $m(\Delta_n)$ by its mean gives mean-one nonnegative variables converging to $m(Z)$, so [F2] makes them uniformly integrable. The means tend to one, hence $(m(\Delta_n))$ is uniformly integrable. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F7, F8, given, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 4.1 For bounded continuous $f$, the predictive law satisfies $E_{M_n}f(\Delta_n)=E_{P_{n,0}}[m_n f(\Delta_n)] =E_{P_{n,0}}[m(\Delta_n)f(\Delta_n)]+o(1).$ For a cutoff $Q$, $(m\wedge Q)f$ is bounded and continuous, so its expectation converges by [F1]. The tail error is at most $\|f\|_\infty E[m(\Delta_n)\mathbf1_{\{m(\Delta_n)>Q\}}]$, which tends uniformly to zero as $Q\to\infty$ by step 1.1. Thus the limit is $E[m(Z)f(Z)]$. This is the Gaussian-shift mixture with base law $N_d(0,K)$ and density $m(z)$. [F1, step 1.1, F3, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$ with positive-definite covariance
$\Sigma$. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable and symmetric,
$L(-x)=L(x)$, and quasi-convex, meaning each sublevel set
$\{x:L(x)\le t\}$ is convex. Then for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$E L(X-a)\ge E L(X-m).$$
Thus the Gaussian center $m$ minimizes expected loss. The result includes
quasi-convex losses whose sublevel sets are not closed.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 First let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be closed, symmetric, and convex. For each radius $r>0$ and shift $v$, put $U=C\cap(v+\overline B(0,r)),\qquad V=C\cap(-v+\overline B(0,r)).$ They are compact convex sets by [F7], and $V=-U$, so they have equal volume by [F5]. For $u\in U$ and $w\in V$, symmetry and convexity put $(u+w)/2$ in $C$, while $u-v$ and $w+v$ lie in the radius-$r$ ball, so $\|(u+w)/2\|_2=\|(u-v+w+v)/2\|_2\le r$. Thus $(U+V)/2\subseteq C\cap\overline B(0,r)$. This sets up the Brunn–Minkowski comparison. [F5, F7, given, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 6.1 For any random variable $Y$ with $0\le Y\le M$, $EY=\int_0^M P(Y>t)dt$, by [F4]. Step 5.1 says $P(L(X-a)\le t)\le P(L(X-m)\le t)$ for each $t$, hence the corresponding tail probabilities are ordered in the reverse direction. Integrating them gives $E L(X-a)\ge E L(X-m)$. This proves the statement without requiring closed loss sublevels. [F4, step 5.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and a parametric model QMD at $\theta_0$ with score $s_{\theta_0}$.
Then
$$E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}=0,$$
and the information matrix
$I_{\theta_0}=E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$ has finite entries
and is positive semidefinite. The QMD convention and square-integrability of
the score are those of [[def-qmd-path]].
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 Fix $v\in\mathbb R^d$ and put $f_t=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+tv}}$, $f_0=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}$. By [F1]–[F2], $f_t-f_0=\tfrac t2(v^Ts)f_0+r_{tv},\qquad \|r_{tv}\|_2=o(|t|).$ Since each density integrates to one, $\|f_t\|_2=\|f_0\|_2=1$, and $0=2\langle f_0,f_t-f_0\rangle+\|f_t-f_0\|_2^2.$ This identity uses the unit norms of the square-root densities. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 3.1 Each $s_j$ is square-integrable under a probability law, so $E|s_j|<\infty$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Also $E|s_js_k|\le(E s_j^2)^{1/2}(E s_k^2)^{1/2}<\infty$; hence every entry of $I_{\theta_0}$ is finite. For any $a\in\mathbb R^d$, $a^TI_{\theta_0}a=E(a^Ts)^2\ge0$, proving positive semidefiniteness, with no nonsingularity assertion. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be LAN at $h=0$ with
positive-definite information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$.
Let $T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ be regular under every fixed
local alternative, with common limit law $W$ as in
[[def-regular-estimator-under-local-alternatives]]. Then there is a
probability law $\nu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ such that
$$\mathcal L(W)=N_d(0,K^{-1})*\nu.$$
Here $*$ is convolution, the law of the sum of independent random vectors
with the two indicated laws. In particular, the efficient Gaussian component
with covariance $K^{-1}$ is a convolution factor of every regular limit.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 Under $P_{n,0}$, $T_n\Rightarrow W$ by regularity at $h=0$ and $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)$ by LAN. By [F4], both marginal sequences are tight. Their joint laws are tight: for any $\epsilon>0$, choose compact balls $C_T,C_\Delta$ with marginal outside probabilities below $\epsilon/2$; the union bound puts the joint law on the compact product with probability at least $1-\epsilon$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F9, given, choose, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 6.1 By [F12], form the product law $\rho=\mathcal L(R)\otimes\mathcal L(\Delta)$ on $\mathbb R^{2d}$. Step 5.1 and factorization of the bounded product integrals show that $\rho$ and $\mathcal L(R,\Delta)$ have identical joint characteristic functions. For every $a,b\in\mathbb R^d$ and real $v$, evaluate these functions at $(va,vb)$; this gives equality of the scalar characteristic functions of the projection $(r,z)\mapsto a^Tr+b^Tz$ under the two laws. Scalar uniqueness [F8] identifies each projection law, and Cramér–Wold [F11], under the existing AC hypothesis [A1], gives $\mathcal L(R,\Delta)=\rho$. Thus $R$ and $\Delta$ are independent. Since $K$ is invertible, $K^{-1}\Delta\sim N_d(0,K^{-1})$, and $T=K^{-1}\Delta+R$. The law of $T$, which is $W$, is therefore $N_d(0,K^{-1})*\mathcal L(R)$, proving the claimed convolution with $\nu=\mathcal L(R)$. [A1, F6, F8, F11, F12, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. In a pointwise LAN experiment [[def-lan-experiment]] with $K\succ0$, fix $h_1,\ldots,h_s\in\mathbb R^d$ and weights $w_i>0$ summing to one. Let $g:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Lipschitz. The Bayes values for estimating $h$ with loss $g(a-h)$ and this finite prior, allowing all measurable randomized rules, converge to the corresponding Bayes value in the Gaussian shift $Y\mid h\sim N_d(h,K^{-1})$. No likelihood-field uniformity or measurable-selection hypothesis is required.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 For $l\in[0,\infty)^s$, set $F(l)=\inf_a\sum_iw_i l_i g(a-h_i)$. For any $l,l'$, each action's objective changes by at most $M\sum_iw_i|l_i-l'_i|$; taking infima proves the same bound for $F$. Also $0\le F(l)\le M\sum_iw_i l_i$. For fixed $l$ the objective is continuous in $a$, so F6 makes its infimum equal to the infimum over a fixed enumeration $(q_j)$ of the rational grid. For $\epsilon>0$, choose the first $j$ whose objective is at most $F(l)+\epsilon$. This index is Borel: its defining set and the finitely many failures at smaller indices are Borel. Thus this is an explicit measurable $\epsilon$-optimal action function of $l$. [F4, F6, given, construct, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 3.1 Under the proxy mixture, the predictive density is $U_n=\sum_iw_iL_{n,h_i}$ and, when $U_n>0$, the posterior weights are $w_iL_{n,h_i}/U_n$. Conditional on the data, every randomized action rule has posterior risk at least $F((L_{n,h_i})_i)/U_n$, because $F$ is the infimum over deterministic actions and randomization averages those action risks. The measurable selector from step 1.1 has posterior risk at most this envelope plus $\epsilon$. Multiplying by the predictive density and integrating shows that the proxy Bayes value differs from $E_{P_{n,0}}F((L_{n,h_i})_i)$ by at most $\epsilon$; the set $U_n=0$ has zero predictive probability. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ identifies the proxy Bayes value with that expectation. The same argument with $l_i(Z)$ identifies the limiting envelope expectation as the finite-prior Gaussian Bayes value: tilting the base Gaussian by $l_i$ gives $Z\sim N_d(Kh_i,K)$, and $Y=K^{-1}Z$ has law $N_d(h_i,K^{-1})$. Finally [F5] bounds the actual/proxy risk difference uniformly over rules by $M\sum_iw_i\|P_{n,h_i}-L_{n,h_i}P_{n,0}\|_{\rm TV}\to0$. Infima preserve this bound, proving the assertion. Assume AC. Let $Q_h=N_d(h,S)$ with $S\succ0$ and let $g:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ have Lipschitz constant $B<\infty$. For every Borel probability prior $\pi$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and $\epsilon>0$, there is a finite-support prior $\pi_f$ whose Bayes value for loss $g(a-h)$ differs from that of $\pi$ by less than $\epsilon$. The comparison is uniform over all measurable randomized rules. In particular this applies to every diffuse Gaussian prior; no posterior selector assumption is needed.

On a fixed bounded set of shifts, the density formula and $\|y-h\|_2^2\ge\|y\|_2^2/2-\|h\|_2^2$ bound all these densities by $C\exp(-c'\|y\|_2^2)$ for constants $C,c'>0$. This is integrable, so [F2] gives $L^1$ convergence; for every event, its probability difference is at most that $L^1$ distance. On a compact ball this continuity is uniform: otherwise there are $h_j,h'_j$ in the ball with $\|h_j-h'_j\|_2\to0$ but TV distances bounded below. Cover this compact ball by open balls of radius $\eta/2$; [F5] gives a finite subcover. Intersect the first ball with the closed ball, then successively remove the previous covering sets from each later intersection. This makes a finite Borel partition whose cells have diameter at most $\eta$. Assign one point to each nonempty cell and send points outside the closed ball to zero. The resulting finite-valued map q is Borel, and $\pi_f=\pi\circ q^{-1}$. On the ball, step 2.1 bounds $|R_\delta(h)-R_\delta(q(h))|$ by $B\eta+M\omega(\eta)$, where the compact-ball TV modulus satisfies $\omega(\eta)\to0$ by step 1.1. Outside, use $M$. Thus prior risks differ uniformly over rules by at most $B\eta+M\omega(\eta)+M\tau$. Choose the ball first for small tail, then the cell diameter small on that fixed ball. ## Statement

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. Let $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be a finite-dimensional
experiment that is LAN at $h=0$ with positive-definite information $K$ and
central sequence $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)$ as in
[[def-lan-experiment]]. Let $M\ge0$ be finite and
$L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable,
symmetric ($L(-x)=L(x)$), and quasi-convex (each sublevel set is convex).
Then
$$ \liminf_{c\to\infty}\liminf_{n\to\infty} \inf_{\widehat h_n}\sup_{\|h\|_2\le c} E_{P_{n,h}}L(\widehat h_n-h) \ge E L(Z),\qquad Z\sim N_d(0,K^{-1}). $$
The infimum ranges over measurable, possibly randomized estimators. The
experiment is pointwise LAN in each fixed $h$; no uniform likelihood-field
assumption is added.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 If $M=0$, then $L$ is identically zero and the claimed bound is equality. Assume $M>0$ for the rest of the proof. Fix arbitrary integers $N\ge2$ and $m\ge1$, and set $g=g_{N,m}$ from [F4]; it is bounded Lipschitz and $g\le L$. For each $\rho>0$, set $\Gamma=\rho^{-1}K^{-1}$, and let $\pi_\Gamma=N_d(0,\Gamma)$. Define $V_{n,c}(g)=\inf_{\widehat h_n}\sup_{\|h\|_2\le c} E_{P_{n,h}}g(\widehat h_n-h)$ and $V(g)=\liminf_{c\to\infty}\liminf_{n\to\infty}V_{n,c}(g)$. If a finite prior $\pi_f$ is supported in the radius-$c$ ball, then every worst-case risk is at least its prior average by [F5]. Taking infima gives $V_{n,c}(g)\ge B_n(\pi_f,g)$, the finite-prior Bayes value. [F4, F5, F6, F8, given, construct, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 5.1 Since $g\le L$, every estimator's risk under $L$ dominates its risk under this fixed $g$, so the local minimax value for $L$ is at least $V(g)$. Step 4.1 gives the lower bound $E g_{N,m}(Z)$. The choices $N,m$ in step 1.1 were arbitrary; first let $m\to\infty$ and then $N\to\infty$. By [F4] these lower bounds converge to $E L(Z)$. This is the stated inequality. [F4, F9, step 1.1, step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $n\ge2$, define probability laws on $\{0,1\}$ by
$$P_n\{1\}=1/n,\qquad Q_n\{1\}=1/2.$$
Then $Q_n$ is not contiguous with respect to $P_n$. The likelihood ratios
$L_n=dQ_n/dP_n$ exist, but their $P_n$-distributional limit has mean less
than one; therefore the matching-mean hypothesis in
[[thm-mean-one-likelihood-ratio-limit-implies-contiguity]] is essential.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 Let $A_n=\{1\}$. Then $P_n(A_n)=1/n\to0$, while $Q_n(A_n)=1/2$ for every $n$. By [F1], this disproves $Q_n\triangleleft P_n$. [F1, given, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 2.1 On the two atoms, the density is $L_n(1)=\frac{Q_n\{1\}}{P_n\{1\}}=\frac n2,\qquad L_n(0)=\frac{Q_n\{0\}}{P_n\{0\}}=\frac{n}{2(n-1)}.$ Under $P_n$, the value $n/2$ occurs with probability $1/n$ and the other value tends to $1/2$, so $L_n\Rightarrow 1/2$. Each $E_{P_n}L_n=1$, but $E(1/2)=1/2\ne1$; hence the matching-mean condition of [F2] fails. [F2, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. A **density version** on $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel
function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d=1.$$
Write $P_f=f\,d\lambda_d$ for its probability law
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Let $\Theta$ be any set of such density
versions. For sample size $n\ge1$, the iid experiment has data space
$$\left((\mathbb R^d)^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\right)$$
and sampling law $P_f^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $f\in\Theta$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]],
[[def-independent-random-elements]],
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
The pointwise target at $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the estimand
$$\psi_x(f)=f(x):\Theta\to\mathbb R$$
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

A **normalized kernel** is a Borel function $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with
$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate
is the indexed family
$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For each fixed $x$, this is intended as a real-valued estimator of $\psi_x$;
the next local lemma supplies its measurability
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]).

Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $K$ is pointwise nonnegative the estimate
is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density
version: this definition does not assert that $f\mapsto f(x)$ is
identifiable from the law $P_f$.

## Statement

derivatives through order two existing and continuous, so
$\int f\,d\lambda_d=1$. If its Hessian satisfies
$H:=\sup_x\|D^2f(x)\|_{op}<\infty$, then $f$ is bounded.

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f$ be a density version in
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d)$, and let $K$ be a normalized Borel kernel with
$K\in L^1$, $\int u_jK(u)\,du=0$ for every $j$, and
$$M_2(K):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|K(u)|\,\|u\|^2du<\infty.$$
Define the convolution $S_hf=\int K(u)f(\cdot-hu)du$ as an $L^2$ equivalence
class. With
$$\|D^2f\|_{2,F}^2:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\|\partial_{jk}f\|_{L^2}^2,$$
one has, for every $h>0$,
$$\|S_hf-f\|_{L^2}\le\frac{h^2}{2}M_2(K)\,\|D^2f\|_{2,F}.$$

The chain rule [F6] gives $q'(0)=-h\nabla g(x)\cdot u$ and $q''(t)=h^2u^TD^2g(x-thu)u$. Integration by parts and the second fundamental theorem [F7] give $g(x-hu)=g(x)-h\nabla g(x)\cdot u+ h^2\int_0^1(1-t)\,u^TD^2g(x-thu)u\,dt.$ The first moments are absolutely integrable since $|u_j|\le1+\|u\|^2$ and $K\in L^1$ with $M_2(K)<\infty$. Integrating against $K(u)$ therefore cancels the constant and linear terms by $\int K=1$ and $\int u_jK(u)du=0$. Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|u^TD^2g(y)u|\le\|u\|\,\|D^2g(y)u\|\le \|u\|^2\|D^2g(y)\|_F$. Apply Holder [F5] with the finite measure $|K(u)|(1-t)\|u\|^2du\,dt$, whose total mass is $M_2(K)/2$, to obtain $|S_hg(x)-g(x)|^2\le h^4\left(\frac{M_2(K)}2\right) \int_{\mathbb R^d}\!\int_0^1 |K(u)|(1-t)\|u\|^2\|D^2g(x-thu)\|_F^2dt\,du.$ Tonelli [F3] and translation invariance from [F4] then give $\|S_hg-g\|_2^2\le h^4\left(\frac{M_2(K)}2\right)^2 \|D^2g\|_{2,F}^2.$ [given, A1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 2.1 For every Borel representative $q\in L^2$, the integrand $(x,u)\mapsto K(u)q(x-hu)$ is product-measurable. If two Borel representatives agree almost everywhere, translation invariance makes their translates agree almost everywhere for each $u$; Tonelli [F3] then makes their convolution integrals agree for almost every $x$. Thus $S_h$ is well-defined as an $L^2$ equivalence class on the classes used here. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $g\in C_c^\infty$ as in [F2]. The finite sum defining $\|D^2(g-f)\|_{2,F}$ is at most $d\|g-f\|_{W^{2,2}}$, so step 1.1 and the operator bound just proved imply $\|S_hf-f\|_2\le(\|K\|_1+1)\epsilon+ \frac{h^2}{2}M_2(K)\big(\|D^2f\|_{2,F}+d\epsilon\big).$ Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves the asserted bound. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with bounded
continuous Borel density version $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$. Let
$K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel, $K\in L^1\cap L^2$, and
$\int K(u)du=1$. For fixed $x\in\mathbb R^d$, along bandwidths $h=h_n>0$
with $h_n\to0$ and $nh_n^d\to\infty$,
$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_{h_n}(x)) =\frac{f(x)\|K\|_2^2}{nh_n^d}+o((nh_n^d)^{-1}).$$

By [F2] and [F7], and using the nonnegative substitution $u\mapsto x-hu$ from [F8], $\mathbb E[Z_i^2]=h^d\int K(u)^2f(x-hu)du \le h^d\|f\|_\infty\|K\|_2^2<\infty.$ Likewise $\mathbb E|Z_i|\le h^d\|f\|_\infty\|K\|_1<\infty$, so each $Z_i$ is integrable and square-integrable. The maps $z\mapsto K((x-z)/h)$ preserve independence by [F4]; identical laws of $X_i$ give identical laws of $Z_i$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F7, F8]

Apply the nonnegative density identity [F7] to each part and subtract using [F11], obtaining $\mathbb EZ_1=\int gf$. Applying the signed substitution [F9] to this integrable product gives $\mathbb E Z_1=h^d\int K(u)f(x-hu)du$, so $|\mathbb EZ_1|\le h^d\|f\|_\infty\|K\|_1$. Along any sequence $h_n\to0$, [F10] gives $\int K(u)^2f(x-h_nu)du\longrightarrow f(x)\|K\|_2^2.$ Thus the first term in step 2.1 is $f(x)\|K\|_2^2/(nh_n^d)+o((nh_n^d)^{-1})$. The subtracted mean-square term is $O(n^{-1})=o((nh_n^d)^{-1})$ because $h_n^d\to0$. The additional $nh_n^d\to\infty$ condition places the expansion in the vanishing-variance regime. This proves the formula. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F7, F9, F10, F11, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with a Borel density
version $f\in W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d)$. Let $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be
Borel, $K\in L^1\cap L^2$, $\int K(u)du=1$,
$\int u_jK(u)du=0$ for every $j$, and
$M_2(K):=\int|K(u)|\|u\|^2du<\infty$. For every $h>0$ define
$$\operatorname{MISE}(\widehat f_h) :=\mathbb E\int_{\mathbb R^d}(\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2dx.$$
Then
$$\operatorname{MISE}(\widehat f_h) \le\frac{h^4}{4}M_2(K)^2\|D^2f\|_{2,F}^2+ \frac{\|K\|_2^2}{nh^d}.$$
In particular, $h_n=n^{-1/(d+4)}$ gives
$\operatorname{MISE}(\widehat f_{h_n})=O(n^{-4/(d+4)})$, where $O(n^{-4/(d+4)})$
means bounded by a finite constant times $n^{-4/(d+4)}$ for all sufficiently
large $n$. This is an upper rate under the displayed hypotheses; it is not a
minimax lower bound.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 For fixed $h$, [F2] makes $(z,x)\mapsto\widehat f_h(x)$ Borel, and [F1] makes $f(x)$ Borel as a function of $(z,x)$. Arithmetic measurability in [F2] therefore makes the squared error product-measurable and nonnegative. Tonelli [F6] identifies MISE with the integral over $x$ of its expected pointwise squared error, even before finiteness has been established. [given, F1, F2, F6]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 4.1 At almost every $x$, expand $\widehat f_h(x)-f(x)=(\widehat f_h(x)-\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x))+(\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))$. The centered term has expectation zero, so [F10]–[F11] give $\mathbb E[(\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2] =\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_h(x)) +(\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2.$ Integrate this nonnegative identity using step 1.1, then apply steps 3.1 and 3.2 to obtain the displayed MISE bound. For $h_n=n^{-1/(d+4)}$, both $h_n^4$ and $(nh_n^d)^{-1}$ equal $n^{-4/(d+4)}$, which proves the stated upper rate. [F10, F11, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

For $d\ge1$, take the standard Gaussian kernel
$$K_d(u)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\|u\|^2/2}.$$
Its second-moment matrix is $\mu_{jk}=\delta_{jk}$ and
$\|K_d\|_2^2=(4\pi)^{-d/2}$, where $\delta_{jk}$ is $1$ for $j=k$ and $0$
otherwise. Thus, under the pointwise theorem hypotheses,
$$\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x)=\tfrac12h^2\Delta f(x)+o(h^2),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_h(x)) =\frac{f(x)}{nh^d}(4\pi)^{-d/2}+o((nh^d)^{-1}).$$
Here $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{jj}f$.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 Put $I=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-t^2}dt$. Tonelli [F2] and [F1] give $I^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-(x^2+y^2)}d(x,y)=\pi$. Since $I\ge0$, $I=\sqrt\pi$. Let $\phi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. The substitution $s=t/\sqrt2$ in [F3] then gives $\int\phi=1$. By [F5], $\phi'(t)=-t\phi(t)$. Integration by parts [F6] gives $\int_0^R t\phi(t)dt=\phi(0)-\phi(R)$. By [F7], $\phi(R)\to0$ and $R\phi(R)\to0$, so $\int|t|\phi(t)dt=2\phi(0)<\infty$. Oddness then gives $\int t\phi(t)dt=0$. Integration by parts [F6] on $[-R,R]$ also yields $\int_{-R}^R t^2\phi(t)dt =\int_{-R}^R\phi(t)dt-[t\phi(t)]_{-R}^R.$ As $R\to\infty$, $R\phi(R)\to0$ by [F7] (put $s=R^2/4$ and use $R\le2s$ for $R\ge2$), and the right side tends to $1$, so $\int t^2\phi(t)dt=1$ by [F9]. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F9]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 3.1 Substituting $\mu_{jk}=\delta_{jk}$ and $\|K_d\|_2^2=(4\pi)^{-d/2}$ into [F8] yields the two displayed leading terms. The Gaussian kernel is nonnegative and integrates to one by step 2.1, so [[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]] also confirms that each finite estimate is a density. [step 2.1, F8, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on it, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, and let $\mu$ be a fixed sigma-finite measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Suppose $(p_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a specified family of nonnegative measurable densities with $\int p_\theta\,d\mu=1$. Let $P$ be the actual data probability measure; it need not equal any model law $p_\theta\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Assume $p_\theta(X)>0$ $P$-almost surely and $\ell_\theta(X):=\log p_\theta(X)$ is integrable under $P$ for every parameter considered. Expectation means integration against $P$ ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

The population log-likelihood criterion is $M_P(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\ell_\theta(X)]$. A **pseudo-true parameter** is any maximizer $\theta^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta\in\Theta}M_P(\theta)$. It is unique when this argmax set is the singleton $\{\theta^*\}$. The model is **misspecified relative to $P$** when $P\ne p_\theta\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. ## Definition

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on it, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, and let $\mu$ be a fixed sigma-finite measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Suppose $(p_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a specified family of nonnegative measurable densities with $\int p_\theta\,d\mu=1$. Let $P$ be the actual data probability measure; it need not equal any model law $p_\theta\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Assume $p_\theta(X)>0$ $P$-almost surely and $\ell_\theta(X):=\log p_\theta(X)$ is integrable under $P$ for every parameter considered. Expectation means integration against $P$ ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

The population log-likelihood criterion is $M_P(\theta):=\mathbb E_P[\ell_\theta(X)]$. A **pseudo-true parameter** is any maximizer $\theta^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\theta\in\Theta}M_P(\theta)$. It is unique when this argmax set is the singleton $\{\theta^*\}$. The model is **misspecified relative to $P$** when $P\ne p_\theta\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. This definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, interiority, or separation of the maximizer; those are theorem hypotheses when needed.

## Definition

Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, $n\ge p+1$, and $a<b$. A clamped knot vector is a nondecreasing finite sequence
$$\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_{p+1}=a<\xi_{p+2}\le\cdots\le\xi_n<\xi_{n+1}=\cdots=\xi_{n+p+1}=b,$$
with $\xi_j<\xi_{j+p+1}$ for every $1\le j\le n$. Empty interior ranges are omitted. The multiplicity $\mu(\eta)$ of an interior knot $\eta$ is its number of occurrences among $\xi_{p+2},\ldots,\xi_n$.

Write $\mathcal P_p$ for the real polynomials of degree at most $p$. The degree-$p$ spline space $S_{p,\xi}$ consists of functions that restrict to a member of $\mathcal P_p$ on each nonempty knot interval and whose derivatives through order $p-\mu(\eta)$ agree across each interior knot $\eta$. The convention $C^{-1}$ means that no matching condition is imposed. For this piecewise definition, take knot cells left-closed and right-open; at a knot with no matching condition, the value is the one from the cell on its right, and at $b$ use the left limit. Thus the function value at a discontinuous knot is specified.

The degree-zero B-spline is $B_{j,0,\xi}=\mathbf 1_{[\xi_j,\xi_{j+1})}$. For $p\ge1$, define recursively
$$B_{j,p,\xi}(x)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}B_{j,p-1,\xi}(x)+\frac{\xi_{j+p+1}-x}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}(x),$$
where a term with zero denominator is defined to be zero. At $b$, set $B_{j,p,\xi}(b)$ equal to its left limit. The basis and regularity properties of this recursively defined family are proved in [[thm-spline-polynomial-reproduction]].

## Definition

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be one measurable space and let $P_n,Q_n$ be
probability measures on it ([[def-probability-measure]]). The sequence
$(Q_n)$ is **contiguous with respect to** $(P_n)$, written $Q_n\triangleleft
P_n$, if for every sequence $A_n\in\mathcal A$,
$$P_n(A_n)\longrightarrow0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q_n(A_n)\longrightarrow0.$$
The sequences are **mutually contiguous**, written $Q_n\triangleleft\triangleright
P_n$, if both $Q_n\triangleleft P_n$ and $P_n\triangleleft Q_n$.

Contiguity is a relation between sequences of laws, not absolute continuity at
each finite $n$. It says that events negligible under one sequence remain
negligible under the other in the indicated direction.

## Definition

Let $P_{n,h}$ be probability laws on a common measurable space for each
integer $n\ge1$ and local parameter $h\in\mathbb R^d$, where $d<\infty$ and
$P_{n,0}$ is the base law. Suppose that for every fixed $h$ we are supplied a
nonnegative measurable function $L_{n,h}$ with
$$\int L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}=1.$$
It defines an absolutely continuous proxy
$$\bar P_{n,h}(A):=\int_A L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}.$$
The actual local law is allowed to have a singular part; the approximation
condition below is what connects it to this proxy.

The experiments are **locally asymptotically normal (LAN)** at $h=0$ with
information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$ if $K$ is a symmetric
positive semidefinite $d\times d$ matrix, $\Delta_n$ is an $\mathbb R^d$-valued
statistic,
$$\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)\quad\text{under }P_{n,0},$$
and for every fixed $h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\|P_{n,h}-\bar P_{n,h}\|_{\rm TV}\to0,\qquad \log L_{n,h}=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TKh+o_{P_{n,0}}(1),$$
where $\|\cdot\|_{\rm TV}$ is the event-supremum total variation distance
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]) and
$o_{P_{n,0}}(1)$ means convergence to zero in $P_{n,0}$-probability. We set
$\log0=-\infty$; the finite-valued expansion entails
$P_{n,0}(L_{n,h}=0)\to0$. Convergence in distribution is as in
[[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], and $N_d(0,K)$ allows
singular $K$ ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

If $P_{n,h}=\bar P_{n,h}$, this is the usual dominated LAN comparison. The
proxy formulation also covers QMD paths whose local alternatives are not
absolutely continuous with respect to the base law, provided the singular
product mass tends to zero in total variation. This definition is pointwise
in each fixed $h$; it does not assert uniformity over bounded sets of $h$.

## Statement

Let $H\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact, let $\pi$ be a probability measure on

in $(h,x)$, nonnegative, and satisfies
$\int L_n(h,x)P_{n,0}(dx)=1$ for every $h\in H$. Let
$\Delta_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_d(0,K)$ under $P_{n,0}$, where $K$ is positive
semidefinite, and put
$$g_h(z)=\exp(h^Tz-\tfrac12h^TKh).$$
Assume the random variable
$$a_n(x):=\sup_{h\in H}|L_n(h,x)-g_h(\Delta_n(x))|$$
is measurable and $E_{P_{n,0}}a_n\to0$. Let the prior-predictive law be
$M_n(dx)=m_n(x)P_{n,0}(dx)$ with
$m_n(x)=\int_HL_n(h,x)\pi(dh)$, and define posteriors
$$\Pi_n(dh\mid x)=\frac{L_n(h,x)\pi(dh)}{m_n(x)},\qquad \Pi^G(dh\mid z)=\frac{g_h(z)\pi(dh)}{m(z)},\quad m(z)=\int_Hg_h(z)\pi(dh),$$
where an arbitrary probability measure is assigned if a denominator is zero.
Then
$$E_{M_n}\int_H\left| \frac{L_n(h,X)}{m_n(X)}- \frac{g_h(\Delta_n(X))}{m(\Delta_n(X))} \right|\pi(dh)\longrightarrow0.$$
In particular the posterior laws converge in expected total variation,
because their event-probability differences are bounded by this $L^1(\pi)$
distance. The convention for total variation is
[[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]].

This lemma assumes an $L^1$ uniform likelihood-field approximation. Pointwise
LAN alone does not supply that hypothesis.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be LAN at $h=0$ with
positive-definite information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$.
Let $T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ be regular under every fixed
local alternative, with common limit law $W$ as in
[[def-regular-estimator-under-local-alternatives]]. Then there is a
probability law $\nu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ such that
$$\mathcal L(W)=N_d(0,K^{-1})*\nu.$$
Here $*$ is convolution, the law of the sum of independent random vectors
with the two indicated laws. In particular, the efficient Gaussian component
with covariance $K^{-1}$ is a convolution factor of every regular limit.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 Under $P_{n,0}$, $T_n\Rightarrow W$ by regularity at $h=0$ and $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)$ by LAN. By [F4], both marginal sequences are tight. Their joint laws are tight: for any $\epsilon>0$, choose compact balls $C_T,C_\Delta$ with marginal outside probabilities below $\epsilon/2$; the union bound puts the joint law on the compact product with probability at least $1-\epsilon$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F9, given, choose, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 6.1 By [F12], form the product law $\rho=\mathcal L(R)\otimes\mathcal L(\Delta)$ on $\mathbb R^{2d}$. Step 5.1 and factorization of the bounded product integrals show that $\rho$ and $\mathcal L(R,\Delta)$ have identical joint characteristic functions. For every $a,b\in\mathbb R^d$ and real $v$, evaluate these functions at $(va,vb)$; this gives equality of the scalar characteristic functions of the projection $(r,z)\mapsto a^Tr+b^Tz$ under the two laws. Scalar uniqueness [F8] identifies each projection law, and Cramér–Wold [F11], under the existing AC hypothesis [A1], gives $\mathcal L(R,\Delta)=\rho$. Thus $R$ and $\Delta$ are independent. Since $K$ is invertible, $K^{-1}\Delta\sim N_d(0,K^{-1})$, and $T=K^{-1}\Delta+R$. The law of $T$, which is $W$, is therefore $N_d(0,K^{-1})*\mathcal L(R)$, proving the claimed convolution with $\nu=\mathcal L(R)$. [A1, F6, F8, F11, F12, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. In a pointwise LAN experiment [[def-lan-experiment]] with $K\succ0$, fix $h_1,\ldots,h_s\in\mathbb R^d$ and weights $w_i>0$ summing to one. Let $g:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Lipschitz. The Bayes values for estimating $h$ with loss $g(a-h)$ and this finite prior, allowing all measurable randomized rules, converge to the corresponding Bayes value in the Gaussian shift $Y\mid h\sim N_d(h,K^{-1})$. No likelihood-field uniformity or measurable-selection hypothesis is required.
source_anchors.relevant_quote_first_step: 1.1 For $l\in[0,\infty)^s$, set $F(l)=\inf_a\sum_iw_i l_i g(a-h_i)$. For any $l,l'$, each action's objective changes by at most $M\sum_iw_i|l_i-l'_i|$; taking infima proves the same bound for $F$. Also $0\le F(l)\le M\sum_iw_i l_i$. For fixed $l$ the objective is continuous in $a$, so F6 makes its infimum equal to the infimum over a fixed enumeration $(q_j)$ of the rational grid. For $\epsilon>0$, choose the first $j$ whose objective is at most $F(l)+\epsilon$. This index is Borel: its defining set and the finitely many failures at smaller indices are Borel. Thus this is an explicit measurable $\epsilon$-optimal action function of $l$. [F4, F6, given, construct, algebra]
source_anchors.relevant_quote_last_step: 3.1 Under the proxy mixture, the predictive density is $U_n=\sum_iw_iL_{n,h_i}$ and, when $U_n>0$, the posterior weights are $w_iL_{n,h_i}/U_n$. Conditional on the data, every randomized action rule has posterior risk at least $F((L_{n,h_i})_i)/U_n$, because $F$ is the infimum over deterministic actions and randomization averages those action risks. The measurable selector from step 1.1 has posterior risk at most this envelope plus $\epsilon$. Multiplying by the predictive density and integrating shows that the proxy Bayes value differs from $E_{P_{n,0}}F((L_{n,h_i})_i)$ by at most $\epsilon$; the set $U_n=0$ has zero predictive probability. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ identifies the proxy Bayes value with that expectation. The same argument with $l_i(Z)$ identifies the limiting envelope expectation as the finite-prior Gaussian Bayes value: tilting the base Gaussian by $l_i$ gives $Z\sim N_d(Kh_i,K)$, and $Y=K^{-1}Z$ has law $N_d(h_i,K^{-1})$. Finally [F5] bounds the actual/proxy risk difference uniformly over rules by $M\sum_iw_i\|P_{n,h_i}-L_{n,h_i}P_{n,0}\|_{\rm TV}\to0$. Infima preserve this bound, proving the assertion. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
