## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $\theta_0\in\Theta_0$. Assume the full-model parameter set $\Theta$ is open in $\mathbb R^d$, so $\theta_0$ is interior for the QMD model. Under $P_{\theta_0}$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID and let $\ell_n(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_\theta(X_i)$ be their sample log-likelihood. Define local parameter sets $C_n:=\sqrt n(\Theta-\theta_0)$ and $C_{0n}:=\sqrt n(\Theta_0-\theta_0)$. Assume the model is QMD at $\theta_0$ as in [[def-qmd-path]], and write $I:=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$ for its Fisher information; assume $I$ is positive definite, meaning $v^TIv>0$ for every nonzero $v$. Suppose $C_n$ and $C_{0n}$ are closed in the Euclidean metric (their complements are open), contain $0$, and converge locally to nonempty closed convex cones $C$ and $C_0$ with $C_0\subseteq C$. A cone contains $0$ and is closed under multiplication by every nonnegative scalar; convex means that the set contains the line segment between each pair of its points. Local convergence means that, for every $R>0$, there are $\delta_{n,R}\to0$ such that every point of $C_n\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ or $C\cap\overline B_2(0,R)$ is within $\delta_{n,R}$ in Euclidean distance of the other set, and likewise for $C_{0n}$ and $C_0$. Here a point $x$ is within $\delta$ of a set $A$ when $\inf_{a\in A}\|x-a\|_2\le\delta$.

Assume a uniform local quadratic likelihood expansion: for $h\in C_n$,

$$\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)=h^TZ_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+r_n(h),$$

where $Z_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_d(0,I)$ under $P_{\theta_0}$ and, for every $R>0$, $\sup\{|r_n(h)|:h\in C_n,\ \|h\|_2\le R\}\to_P0$. Assume the full and null local log-likelihoods attain maxima at $\hat h_n\in C_n$ and $\hat h_{0n}\in C_{0n}$ and that both maximizer sequences are tight, meaning that for every $\eta>0$ some $R<\infty$ makes the limiting upper probability of either norm exceeding $R$ at most $\eta$. For

$$T_n:=2\left[\sup_{h\in C_n}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}-\sup_{h\in C_{0n}}\{\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)\}\right],$$

the likelihood-ratio statistic satisfies

$$T_n\Rightarrow d_I^2(I^{-1}Z,C_0)-d_I^2(I^{-1}Z,C),$$

where $d_I$ is the Fisher-information distance of [[def-fisher-information-metric-distance]]. QMD alone is not asserted to imply the uniform expansion or tightness hypotheses.

anchors.quote:
Let $P$ be a probability measure on a measurable observation space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, and let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$; IID means a common law and mutual independence of the whole family ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). Let $(\Theta,d)$ be a metric candidate space with its Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-metric-space]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For each $\theta\in\Theta$, let $m_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and assume $P|m_\theta|<\infty$. Define
$$P_nm_\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n m_\theta(X_i),\qquad Pm_\theta=\int m_\theta\,dP.$$

A measurable estimator sequence $\hat\theta_n$ into the Borel target $\Theta$ is an **M-estimator** if it maximizes or minimizes $\theta\mapsto P_nm_\theta$; measurability is as in [[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]]. It is an exact maximizer when $P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta$, and an $o_P(1)$-approximate maximizer when the finite measurable gap $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta-P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}$ is $o_P(1)$. For minimization use the gap $P_nm_{\hat\theta_n}-\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}P_nm_\theta$. The notation $o_P(1)$ is that of [[def-op-and-little-op-stochastic-bounds]].

The maximizing and minimizing forms are both included; replacing $m_\theta$ by $-m_\theta$ converts one to the other. This definition does not assert that a maximizer exists, nor that the population criterion $Pm_\theta$ has a unique maximizer. Whenever a random candidate is substituted into the empirical or population criterion, assume that evaluation is measurable and finite.

anchors.quote:
Let $\mathcal Q$ be a family of probability laws on a common measurable sample space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$, and let $\Sigma(Q)\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be a specified matrix parameter for each $Q\in\mathcal Q$, with fixed $p\ge1$. Give $\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ its usual Euclidean topology and Borel sigma-algebra. An estimator is a measurable map $\widehat\Sigma:(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)\to(\mathbb R^{p\times p},\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{p\times p}))$. Define its squared operator risk at $Q$ and the minimax risk over $\mathcal Q$ by
$$R_Q(\widehat\Sigma)=\mathbb E_Q\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(Q)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2,\qquad\mathfrak R(\mathcal Q)=\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{Q\in\mathcal Q}R_Q(\widehat\Sigma).$$

For a family $\mathcal P$ of one-observation laws on a common measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and an integer $n\ge1$, the $n$-observation experiment observes $n$ independent observations, each with law $P$. Its sample space is $(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})$ and its sample law is the finite product probability measure $P^{\otimes n}$; this is the joint law of the IID family in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and [[def-independent-random-elements]]. For estimators $\widehat\Sigma:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathbb R^{p\times p},\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{p\times p}))$, define
$$R_{n,P}(\widehat\Sigma)=\mathbb E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2,\qquad\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P)=\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}R_{n,P}(\widehat\Sigma).$$

An infinite expectation is allowed, so every measurable estimator has an extended nonnegative risk. Suprema of risks are taken in the ordered range $[0,\infty]$, with $\sup\varnothing:=0$, its least element. Thus when $\mathcal Q$ or $\mathcal P$ is empty the corresponding supremum is zero for every estimator, and its minimax risk is zero. The estimator class is nonempty because the constant zero matrix map is measurable. The operator norm is from [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

The oracle-centered sample covariance and the sample-centered covariance are respectively
$$\widehat\Sigma_\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)(X_i-\mu)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat\Sigma^\ast=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T},\quad \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
For a matrix estimate $A$, squared operator loss is $\|A-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, with the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. This definition distinguishes the known-mean raw second moment from the estimator that removes an unknown mean.

anchors.quote:
Assume AC for the supplied density representatives in
[[def-score-and-fisher-information]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid from a dominated parametric model on an open
$\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$, and let $\ell_n(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log
p_\theta(X_i)$. For any nested null $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$ for which the
maxima exist, the **likelihood-ratio statistic** is
$$L_n=2\left\{\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\ell_n(\theta)-\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\ell_n(\theta)\right\}.$$

For the Wald and score statistics, specialize to a **regular equality null of
codimension $q$** at an interior point $\theta_0$: this is a null set which,
in a $C^1$ local parameter chart
$\theta=(\psi,\eta)\in\mathbb R^q\times\mathbb R^{d-q}$, is $\psi=0$ near
$\theta_0=(0,\eta_0)$. Its local tangent is the $\eta$-coordinate subspace.
Assume the QMD information $I(\theta_0)$ is positive definite. Let
$\hat\theta_n$ maximize $\ell_n$ over the full local model and
$\tilde\theta_n$ maximize it over the null, so the general likelihood-ratio
definition is $L_n=2\{\ell_n(\hat\theta_n)-\ell_n(\tilde\theta_n)\}$.

For the score statistic, assume $\log p_\theta(x)$ is differentiable in the
local chart at the parameter values where it is evaluated, and write
$s_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x)$. Require explicitly that this
pointwise derivative at $\theta_0$ agrees $P_{\theta_0}$-almost surely with
the QMD score; this compatibility is an assumption, not a consequence of QMD
alone. The pointwise score and its information-matrix convention are those in
[[def-score-and-fisher-information]].

Partition the score and information in $(\psi,\eta)$ coordinates:
$s=(s_\psi,s_\eta)$ and
$$I=\begin{pmatrix}I_{\psi\psi}&I_{\psi\eta}\\I_{\eta\psi}&I_{\eta\eta}\end{pmatrix},\qquad I_{\mathrm{eff}}=I_{\psi\psi}-I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}.$$
The matrix $I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the information for the tested coordinates
after accounting for the nuisance coordinates. If $d=q$, interpret empty-block
products as zero, so $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=I_{\psi\psi}=I$ and $C$ below is the
empty $q\times0$ matrix. If $d>q$, then $I_{\eta\eta}$ is positive definite;
for $z\ne0$, the quadratic form of $I$ at
$(z,-I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}z)$ equals
$z^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}z>0$. Thus $I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is positive definite in
either case. Put
$$
U_n(\theta)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n s_\theta(X_i).
$$
For a consistent estimator $\widehat I_{\mathrm{eff},n}$ of
$I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and a consistent estimator $\widehat C_n$ of
$C=I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}$, set
$U_{\mathrm{eff},n}=U_{\psi,n}(\tilde\theta_n)-
\widehat C_nU_{\eta,n}(\tilde\theta_n)$. The **score statistic** is
$S_n=U_{\mathrm{eff},n}^T\widehat I_{\mathrm{eff},n}^{-1}U_{\mathrm{eff},n}$.
For a consistent covariance estimator $\widehat V_{\psi,n}$ of the
$\psi$-block of $I^{-1}$, the **Wald statistic** is
$W_n=n\hat\psi_n^T\widehat V_{\psi,n}^{-1}\hat\psi_n$, where
$\hat\psi_n$ is the tested coordinate of $\hat\theta_n$. When a displayed
inverse does not exist, set that statistic to zero; under the regularity
conditions used in the later calibration theorem, the inverse exists with
probability tending to one. This definition gives the statistics and their
normalizations; it asserts no finite-sample or asymptotic distribution.

anchors.quote:
Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$ ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]), and let $(\Theta,d)$ be a metric candidate space with its Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-metric-space]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Fix a finite integer $q\ge1$ and a norm on $\mathbb R^q$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$, let $\psi_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^q$ be measurable with $P\|\psi_\theta\|<\infty$. Define
$$\Psi_n(\theta)=P_n\psi_\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_\theta(X_i),\qquad \Psi(\theta)=P\psi_\theta.$$

A measurable estimator sequence $\hat\theta_n$ into the Borel target $\Theta$ is a **Z-estimator** if it is an exact or $o_P(1)$-approximate root: $\Psi_n(\hat\theta_n)=0$ for every $n$, or $\|\Psi_n(\hat\theta_n)\|=o_P(1)$. Measurability is as in [[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]], and $o_P(1)$ has the convention of [[def-op-and-little-op-stochastic-bounds]]. Whenever a random candidate is substituted into an estimating equation, assume the evaluation is measurable.

Because $q\ge1$ is finite, [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] gives constants $c,C>0$ with $c\|v\|_2\le\|v\|\le C\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^q$. Thus for every $\mathbb R^q$-valued sequence, convergence of the chosen-norm tails to zero is equivalent to the Euclidean $o_P(1)$ convention in [[def-op-and-little-op-stochastic-bounds]].

This definition does not infer a Z-estimating equation from an M-criterion. Differentiating an M-criterion is justified only under additional differentiability and interior-point hypotheses; a nonsmooth criterion need not have a score equation.

anchors.quote:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be an IID sample from a law $P$ on $\mathbb R$ with $P|X|<\infty$. For a realized sample $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, let $x_{(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{(n)}$ be the order statistics and maximize
$$P_nm_\theta=-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i-\theta|,\qquad \theta\in\mathbb R.$$
If $n=2k+1$, the unique maximizer is $x_{(k+1)}$. If $n=2k$, the full maximizing set is $[x_{(k)},x_{(k+1)}]$. Choosing the middle order statistic for odd $n$ and the midpoint of the two middle order statistics for even $n$ gives a measurable exact M-estimator.

1.2 Put $Q(\theta)=\sum_i|x_i-\theta|$. For $n=2k+1$ and $\theta<x_{(k+1)}$, let $\delta=x_{(k+1)}-\theta>0$. Moving to $x_{(k+1)}$ decreases each of the k+1 distances for indices $i\ge k+1$ by exactly $\delta$; each of the other k distances can increase by at most $\delta$ by the triangle inequality. Therefore $Q(x_{(k+1)})-Q(\theta)\le k\delta-(k+1)\delta=-\delta<0$. For $\theta>x_{(k+1)}$, the k+1 distances for indices $i\le k+1$ decrease by $\delta=\theta-x_{(k+1)}$, while each of the other k distances can increase by at most $\delta$, giving the same strict inequality. Thus the odd-sample median uniquely minimizes $Q$. [A1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $n=2k$ and $\theta\in[x_{(k)},x_{(k+1)}]$, the first k observations lie at or below $\theta$ and the last k lie at or above it, so $Q(\theta)=k\theta-\sum_{i=1}^k x_{(i)}+\sum_{i=k+1}^{2k}x_{(i)}-k\theta$ is constant on this interval. If $\theta<x_{(k)}$, moving to $x_{(k)}$ decreases the k+1 distances for $i\ge k$ by $\delta=x_{(k)}-\theta$, while the other k-1 distances can increase by at most $\delta$; hence $Q(x_{(k)})-Q(\theta)\le(k-1)\delta-(k+1)\delta=-2\delta<0$. If $\theta>x_{(k+1)}$, moving to $x_{(k+1)}$ decreases the k+1 distances for $i\le k+1$ by $\delta=\theta-x_{(k+1)}$, while the other k-1 distances can increase by at most $\delta$, so $Q(x_{(k+1)})-Q(\theta)\le-2\delta<0$. Therefore the interval is exactly the minimizing set of $Q$ and the maximizing set of $P_nm_\theta$ by [F1]. [A1, F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

anchors.quote: Let $0<p\le1$ and let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID Bernoulli$(p)$. Write $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. Take $\Theta=\{0,1\}$ with distance $d(\theta,\eta)=|\theta-\eta|$, and set $m_0(x)=0$ and $m_1(x)=x$. Let $\hat\theta_n=1$ when $\bar X_n>0$ and $\hat\theta_n=0$ when $\bar X_n=0$. Then $\hat\theta_n$ is an exact M-estimator and is consistent for the unique population maximizer $\theta_0=1$. This finite criterion class has a uniform law; the proof below gives the Bernoulli strong law directly.

1.2 Independence and the Bernoulli finite sample law imply that expectations of products of functions of distinct coordinates factor: the joint mass at each $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n$ is $\prod_iP(X_i=x_i)$, and summing this product over the finite sample space factors. Expanding $(\sum_iY_i)^4$, every term with an index occurring once has expectation zero by $EY_i=0$ and this factorization; the remaining terms are $\sum_iEY_i^4+6\sum_{i<j}EY_i^2EY_j^2\le n+6\binom n2\le3n^2$. Since $Z\ge0$ implies $P(Z>t)\le EZ/t$ for $t>0$, applying this to $Z=(\sum_iY_i)^4$ gives $P(|\bar X_n-p|>\varepsilon)\le3/(n^2\varepsilon^4)$. [A1, A2, F2, algebra]

2.1 For fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the bound in step 1.2 is summable in $n$. By the union bound, $P(\bigcup_{n\ge N}\{|\bar X_n-p|>\varepsilon\})\le\sum_{n\ge N}3/(n^2\varepsilon^4)\to0$; hence only finitely many such deviations occur almost surely. Applying this to $\varepsilon=1/j$ for every positive integer $j$ gives $\bar X_n\to p$ almost surely. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 Since $p>0$, step 2.1 implies that almost surely $\bar X_n>0$ for every sufficiently large $n$, so $\hat\theta_n=1$ eventually almost surely. In particular, for every $\varepsilon>0$, $P(d(\hat\theta_n,1)>\varepsilon)\to0$, which is consistency by [F3] using the metric in [F4]. Also $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|M_n(\theta)-M(\theta)|=|\bar X_n-p|\to0$ almost surely, displaying the finite-class uniform law. [A1, A2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, given] ∎

$$\sqrt n\{\log T_n-\log1\}\Rightarrow Z.$$
Thus the log transformation has first-order scale $\sqrt n$ and derivative $g'(1)=1$ in this example.
1.1 By [A1], $Z\in\{-1,1\}$. For $n\ge4$, $1+Z/\sqrt n\ge1-1/2=1/2$, so $T_n=1+Z/\sqrt n$ and $\sqrt n(T_n-1)=Z$ exactly. Hence $\sqrt n(T_n-1)\Rightarrow Z$. [A1, given, algebra]

anchors.quote:
Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with known
$\sigma>0$, and test $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ in the one-dimensional location model.
The sample mean is the unique MLE. In this model, the Wald, score, and
likelihood-ratio statistics are exactly equal to
$n(\bar X-\mu_0)^2/\sigma^2$, which has the exact $\chi_1^2$ law under $H_0$.
The notation $\chi_1^2$ is as in [[def-chi-square-law]]. This is a
special finite-sample identity and does not make the general calibration
theorem exact.

1.1 Put $q_\mu(x)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(4\sigma^2)}$. Direct differentiation gives $q'_\mu=(x-\mu)q_\mu/(2\sigma^2)$ and $q''_\mu=((x-\mu)^2/(4\sigma^4)-1/(2\sigma^2))q_\mu$. Its square is a polynomial times $p_\mu=q_\mu^2$. By [F11] and [F12], $\int (x-\mu)^2p_\mu\,dx=\sigma^2$ and $\int (x-\mu)^4p_\mu\,dx=3\sigma^4$, so $\|q''_\mu\|_2^2=3/(16\sigma^4)<\infty$. Also $s_\mu=2q'_\mu/q_\mu=(x-\mu)/\sigma^2$ has second moment $1/\sigma^2$. The identity $q''_a(x)=q''_0(x-a)$ and [F15] give the same norm for every real shift $a$. The two-variable functions $(x,v)\mapsto q''_{\mu+v}(x)$ and $(x,u)\mapsto q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ are continuous. To verify the needed product measurability locally, the rectangles $(a,b)\times(c,d)$ with rational endpoints form a countable base of $\mathbb R^2$: inside any open ball about a point, density of the rationals gives a rational rectangle containing that point and contained in the ball. Every open subset is therefore the union of the subfamily of these rectangles contained in it, hence a countable union of measurable product rectangles. Thus preimages of open subsets under these continuous functions belong to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, and also to the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras. Their squares and restrictions to compact parameter intervals are consequently product measurable, as required by Tonelli below. [F11, F12, F15, given, algebra, F1]

2.1 For fixed $x$, the functions $v\mapsto q''_{\mu+v}(x)$ and $u\mapsto q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ are continuous on each compact interval. By [F13] they are Riemann integrable, by [F9] their integrals are respectively $q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ and $q_{\mu+t}(x)-q_\mu(x)-tq'_\mu(x)$, and [F14] identifies these with their Lebesgue integrals under the assumed AC. Reversed endpoints give the same identities for negative $u,t$. [F13, F9, F14, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Cauchy–Schwarz [F7] on the interval between $0$ and $u$, then Tonelli [F8] and step 1.1, gives $\|q'_{\mu+u}-q'_\mu\|_2^2\le u^2\|q''_0\|_2^2$. The second identity of step 2.1 and another Cauchy–Schwarz/Tonelli application give $\|q_{\mu+t}-q_\mu-tq'_\mu\|_2^2\le |t|\int_0^{|t|}u^2\|q''_0\|_2^2du=|t|^4\|q''_0\|_2^2/3=o(t^2)$. For negative $t$ use $q'_{\mu-u}$ on the length-$|t|$ interval; the same first bound holds. This proves QMD with the explicitly supplied normal densities, score $s_\mu$, and positive information $1/\sigma^2$ by [F5]. [F7, F8, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The log likelihood is a constant minus $(2\sigma^2)^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2$. The identity $\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2+n(\mu-\bar X)^2$ proves $\hat\mu=\bar X$. Since $\sigma^2$ is known, take the exact covariance and information estimates $\widehat V=\sigma^2$ and $\widehat I_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/\sigma^2$; the Wald statistic is $W_n=n(\bar X-\mu_0)^2/\sigma^2$. At the point null the efficient score is $n^{-1/2}\sum_i(X_i-\mu_0)/\sigma^2$, with information $1/\sigma^2$; [F6] gives $S_n=n(\bar X-\mu_0)^2/\sigma^2$. The constrained MLE is $\mu_0$, so twice the log-likelihood difference gives $L_n=n(\bar X-\mu_0)^2/\sigma^2$. [F6, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Under $H_0$, put $Z_n=\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu_0)/\sigma$. The affine and independent-sum characteristic-function identities [F3], together with [F2], give $\mathbb E e^{itZ_n}=\prod_i\mathbb E e^{it(X_i-\mu_0)/(\sigma\sqrt n)} =[e^{-t^2/(2n)}]^n=e^{-t^2/2}$. By [F4], $Z_n\sim N(0,1)$, so $W_n=S_n=L_n=Z_n^2$ has the $\chi_1^2$ law by [F10]. The use of AC is exactly that recorded in [A1]. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F10, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

anchors.quote: Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$, where $P|X|<\infty$ and $PX^2<\infty$. Let $\Theta=\mathbb R$ with its usual metric and set $m_\theta(x)=-(x-\theta)^2$. For a finite observed sample $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the empirical criterion $P_nm_\theta$ has the unique maximizer $\bar x_n=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i$. The population criterion $Pm_\theta$ has the unique maximizer $\mu=PX$. The map from a sample to $\bar x_n$ is measurable, so it is an exact M-estimator.

1.2 Let $\mu=PX$. Expanding $X-\theta=(X-\mu)+(\mu-\theta)$ and using $P(X-\mu)=0$ gives $Pm_\theta=-P[(X-\mu)^2]-(\theta-\mu)^2$. The moment assumptions make the mean and centered second moment finite, so this is uniquely maximized at $\mu$. [A2, given, algebra]

2.1 The IID sequence in [F4] gives the repeated-sampling context. If every coordinate of $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ differs by less than $\delta$, then $|\bar x_n(x)-\bar x_n(y)|\le n^{-1}\sum_i|x_i-y_i|<\delta$. Hence the sample-mean map is continuous for the product topology. Inverse images of open sets are open, so the map is Borel measurable under [A1]; it is an estimator sequence by [F2] and is an exact M-estimator by [F1] and step 1.1. The target metric is the usual metric in [F3]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

Give $\Omega=\{-1,1\}^2$ equal mass $1/4$ at each point, and let $Z=(Z_1,Z_2)$ be the coordinate vector. Put $\theta=(1,2)$, $T_n=\theta+n^{-1/2}Z$, and define $g(x,y)=x/y$ for $y\ne0$ and $g(x,0)=0$. The denominator of $g(T_n)$ is positive for every $n$. The first-order delta method gives

Assume AC. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid real random variables with $\mathbb E|X_1|^4<\infty$. Put $\mu_j=\mathbb E[X_1^j]$ for $1\le j\le4$, $\sigma^2=\mu_2-\mu_1^2$, $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$, $Q_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i^2$, and $S_n^2=Q_n-\bar X_n^2$. Then
$$\sqrt n(S_n^2-\sigma^2)\Rightarrow N_1(0,\tau^2),\qquad \tau^2=\operatorname{Var}((X_1-\mu_1)^2)=\mathbb E[(X_1-\mu_1)^4]-\sigma^4=\mu_4-4\mu_1\mu_3+8\mu_1^2\mu_2-4\mu_1^4-\mu_2^2.$$
Here $\sigma^4=(\sigma^2)^2$ and $\tau^2=\operatorname{Var}((X_1-\mu_1)^2)$.

1.1 Let $Y_i=(X_i,X_i^2)$. The map $x\mapsto(x,x^2)$ is Borel, so [F1]–[F2] show that $(Y_i)$ is iid. By [A2], $\mathbb E\|Y_1\|^2=\mu_2+\mu_4<\infty$, with mean $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ and covariance $$C=\begin{pmatrix}\mu_2-\mu_1^2&\mu_3-\mu_1\mu_2\\\mu_3-\mu_1\mu_2&\mu_4-\mu_2^2\end{pmatrix}.$$ By [A1] and [F3], $\sqrt n\{(\bar X_n,Q_n)-(\mu_1,\mu_2)\}\Rightarrow Z\sim N_2(0,C)$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F6]

2.1 The map $g(x,y)=y-x^2$ has $g(\mu_1,\mu_2)=\sigma^2$ and derivative $(u,v)\mapsto-2\mu_1u+v$. Apply [F5] to step 1.1 to get $\sqrt n(S_n^2-\sigma^2)\Rightarrow-2\mu_1Z_1+Z_2$. [F5, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 By [F4], the limit is centered normal with variance $(-2\mu_1,1)C(-2\mu_1,1)^T=4\mu_1^2(\mu_2-\mu_1^2)-4\mu_1(\mu_3-\mu_1\mu_2)+\mu_4-\mu_2^2=\mu_4-4\mu_1\mu_3+8\mu_1^2\mu_2-4\mu_1^4-\mu_2^2$. anchors.quote:
Assume AC, as inherited through [[thm-fano-packing]]. For every $n\ge1$,
$p\ge2$, $\tau>0$, $0\le q<1$ and $c\ge0$, the minimax squared operator
risk of [[def-minimax-squared-operator-risk]] over
$\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]] satisfies
$$\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P_q(\tau,c))\ge b\tau^2\min\{1,\log(p)/n\},$$
for an absolute constant $b>0$. In particular, the lower bound applies when
$c=0$ and when an effective sparse-row count rounds to zero.

1.1 Put $s=\tau/4$ and $\delta=\tfrac12\min\{1,\sqrt{\log(p+1)/n}\}$. Use $p+1$ Gaussian laws $P_0=N(0,sI_p)$ and $P_j=N(0,s(I_p+\delta e_je_j^{\mathsf T}))$, $1\le j\le p$. Each covariance has operator norm at most $3\tau/8<\tau$. If $Z$ is standard normal, $P(|Z|>t)=e^{-t^2/2}\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-w^2/2-tw}dw\le e^{-t^2/2}$. Hence every unit-direction projection of these laws obeys the required tail with parameter $\tau$. Their covariance matrices are diagonal, so [F2] puts every law in every class in the statement. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For $j\ge1$, the Gaussian covariance KL formula with $\Sigma_j=s(I_p+\delta e_je_j^{\mathsf T})$ and $\Sigma_0=sI_p$ gives $$D(P_j\|P_0)=\tfrac12(\delta-\log(1+\delta))\le\delta^2/4,$$ where $\delta-\log(1+\delta)=\int_0^\delta t/(1+t)\,dt\le\delta^2/2$. By finite-product KL additivity, $$D(P_j^{\otimes n}\|P_0^{\otimes n})=nD(P_j\|P_0)\le n\delta^2/4\le\log(p+1)/16.$$ The $j=0$ divergence is zero, so the reference-law average KL has the same bound. [given, F1, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Use the full matrix action space $\mathcal T=\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ and set $\rho(A,B)=\|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. For a unit vector $v$, rowwise Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] gives $\|Av\|_2^2\le\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2=\|A\|_F^2$, so [F4] gives $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_F$. Conversely each coordinate unit vector $e_j$ has norm one, so $\|A\|_F^2=\sum_j\|Ae_j\|_2^2\le p\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$. Thus $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_F\le\sqrt p\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. The maximum definition also gives homogeneity, symmetry under $A\mapsto-A$, and $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ by the Euclidean triangle inequality on each unit vector. If $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=0$, all columns $Ae_j$ vanish, so $A=0$. Hence $\rho$ is a finite metric by [F5]. The two norm inequalities imply each ball for either metric contains a ball for the other about the same center, so their open sets and therefore their Borel sigma-algebras coincide. Under the entry-list identification $\mathbb R^{p\times p}=\mathbb R^{p^2}$ this is exactly the Euclidean Borel action space in the minimax-risk definition. In particular the diagonal embedding $a\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(a)$ is continuous: its Frobenius difference norm is $\|a-b\|_2$, and its operator difference norm is at most that. All targets in step 1.1 are thus legitimate Borel metric-space points, and every estimator in the minimax definition is measurable into this metric Borel space and induces an admissible deterministic kernel by [F6]. No new choice axiom is used. [given, F4, F5, F6, algebra, step 1.1]

3.1 For a diagonal matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(a)$ and a unit vector $v$, $\|Dv\|_2^2=\sum_j a_j^2v_j^2\le\max_j|a_j|^2$; equality holds at a coordinate unit vector attaining the finite maximum. Hence $\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_j|a_j|$. A target difference from the base has one diagonal entry $s\delta$; a difference between two nonbase targets has two entries $s\delta,-s\delta$. Every distinct pair therefore has metric separation exactly $s\delta$. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F3] to these $p+1$ targets, with the base sample law as reference. Its bracket is at least $1-1/16-\log2/\log3>1/4$. Thus the risk is at least $s^2\delta^2/16\ge(\tau^2/1024)\min\{1,\log p/n\}$. These finite experiments are subsets of the full class, so the full minimax risk is no smaller. [given, F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

anchors.quote:
Let $X$ be a centered real random variable and let $\tau>0$. If
$$\mathbb P(|X|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}\qquad(t>0),$$
then $X$ is sub-Gaussian with proxy $64\tau$ in the MGF convention of [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]]:
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{32\tau\lambda^2}\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb R).$$

1.2 Let $X_1,X_2$ be the coordinate variables on the product of two copies of the law of $X$; [F2] gives this probability space, and its rectangle formula makes them independent with law equal to that of $X$. Set $D=X_1-X_2$. Independence [F3] gives $\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}=(\mathbb E e^{\lambda X})(\mathbb E e^{-\lambda X})$. By [F4], the second factor is at least $1$, so $\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}$. The product is unchanged when $\lambda$ is replaced by $-\lambda$, hence $\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}=\mathbb E\cosh(\lambda D)$. [F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 A union bound gives $\mathbb P(|D|>t)\le4e^{-t^2/(8\tau)}$ because $|D|>t$ implies $|X_1|>t/2$ or $|X_2|>t/2$. For $m\ge1$, [F1] and the substitution $u=t^2/(8\tau)$ yield $\mathbb E|D|^{2m}=2m\int_0^\infty t^{2m-1}\mathbb P(|D|>t)\,dt\le4(8\tau)^m m!.$ The integral is evaluated using $\int_0^\infty t^{2m-1}e^{-t^2/(8\tau)}dt=\tfrac12(8\tau)^m(m-1)!$. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By [F5], the nonnegative power series for $\cosh$ may be integrated term by term. With $x=8\tau\lambda^2$, step 2.1 and $(2m)!\ge(m!)^2$ give $\mathbb E\cosh(\lambda D)\le1+4\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{x^m}{m!}=4e^x-3\le e^{4x}.$ For the last inequality, $f(x)=e^{4x}-4e^x+3$ satisfies $f(0)=0$ and $f'(x)=4(e^{4x}-e^x)\ge0$ for $x\ge0$. Therefore $\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{32\tau\lambda^2}$ for every $\lambda$, which is the proxy-$64\tau$ assertion by [F6]. [F5, F6, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

anchors.quote:
Assume AC. Fix $\tau,M>0$, $\beta>1$, and $0\le q<1$. There are
$v,b>0$ and $P_0<\infty$, depending only on these fixed parameters, such
that the following holds. Let $p\ge P_0$, $n\ge1$, $p\ge n^\beta$ and
$$0\le c\le M n^{(1-q)/2}(\log p)^{-(3-q)/2}.$$
Put $a=\log(p)/n$, $s=\tau/4$, $\epsilon=v\sqrt a$ and
$$k=\left\lfloor\frac{c}{2(s\epsilon)^q}\right\rfloor.$$
If $c/[2(s\epsilon)^q]\ge2$, then
$$\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P_q(\tau,c))\ge b c^2a^{1-q}.$$
For $q=0$, $(s\epsilon)^q=1$. The proof gives all Gaussian mixture and
conditional remainder estimates locally; no external mixture-affinity lemma
is assumed.

1.1 Choose $v^2<(\beta-1)/(4\beta)$ and put $r=\lfloor p/2\rfloor$. Write $x=c/[2(s\epsilon)^q]$, so $x\ge2$ and $k=\lfloor x\rfloor\ge x/2\ge2$. The radius condition gives $x\le C\sqrt n/(\log p)^{3/2}$, hence $k^2\le Cn/(\log p)^3$, $k\epsilon\le C/\log p$, and $n\epsilon^4k^2\le C/\log p$. Also $k^2p^{2v^2}/r\le Cp^{1/\beta+2v^2-1}/(\log p)^3\to0$, uniformly over admitted $n,c$. All constants depend only on fixed parameters. Increase $P_0$ so $r\ge16k$, $2k\epsilon\le1/3$, and the small bounds below hold. Let $\Lambda$ be all $r\times r$ zero-one matrices with every row sum $k$ and every column sum at most $2k$; cyclic shifts of a $k$-set show it is nonempty. For $\gamma\in\{0,1\}^r$, embed $D_\gamma\lambda$ as the upper-right block of a symmetric off-diagonal matrix $A(\gamma,\lambda)$, using two disjoint $r$-coordinate blocks and an extra zero coordinate if $p$ is odd, and put $\Sigma_{\gamma,\lambda}=s(I_p+\epsilon A(\gamma,\lambda))$. Every absolute row sum of $A$ is at most $2k$. For any $z$, $|z^{\mathsf T}Az|\le\frac12\sum_{j,l}|A_{jl}|(z_j^2+z_l^2)\le2k\|z\|_2^2$; applying this to unit eigenvectors and using [F4] bounds the eigenvalues of $A$ in $[-2k,2k]$. Thus $\Sigma_{\gamma,\lambda}$ is positive definite with eigenvalues in $[2s/3,4s/3]\subset(0,\tau]$. Each column has at most $2k$ off-diagonal entries of magnitude $s\epsilon$. If $0<q<1$, its weak-$\ell_q$ quantity is at most $2k(s\epsilon)^q\le c$; if $q=0$, its nonzero count is at most $2k\le c$. Hence [F2] puts every covariance in the radius-$c$ class. The standard-normal density gives $P(|Z|>t)=e^{-t^2/2}\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-w^2/2-tw}\,dw\le e^{-t^2/2}$, so [F1] verifies the directional-tail condition. For any rectangular matrix $M$ and vector $z$, [F5] gives $|(Mz)_i|^2\le(\sum_j|M_{ij}|)(\sum_j|M_{ij}|z_j^2)$. Summing over rows yields $\|Mz\|_2^2\le(\max_i\sum_j|M_{ij}|)(\max_j\sum_i|M_{ij}|)\|z\|_2^2$, hence $\|M\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\le(\max_i\sum_j|M_{ij}|)(\max_j\sum_i|M_{ij}|)$. Therefore each cross-block matrix $C=\epsilon D_{\gamma_{-1}}L$ below has $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sqrt2k\epsilon\le2k\epsilon$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, algebra, construct]

2.1 Give $(\gamma,\lambda)$ the uniform prior on $\{0,1\}^r\times\Lambda$. Fix bit $i$, say $i=1$ by row symmetry, and condition on the remaining bit vector $\gamma_{-1}$ and nuisance rows $L=(\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_r)$. The number of possible first-row supports is $N(L)=\binom{d(L)}k$, where $d(L)$ counts columns whose nuisance sum is less than $2k$. Since there are $(r-1)k$ nuisance ones, $d(L)\ge r/2$. The marginal prior of $L$ is $\pi(L)=N(L)/|\Lambda|$, independent of $\gamma_{-1}$; conditional on $L$, a support $A$ is uniform among its $N(L)$ available $k$-sets. For each fixed $\gamma_{-1}$, when $\gamma_1=0$ let $Q_{\gamma_{-1},L}$ be the Gaussian n-sample law, which does not depend on $A$; when $\gamma_1=1$, let $P_{\gamma_{-1},A,L}$ be the n-sample law and $\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L}$ its uniform support mixture. In the chi-square expansion draw two independent available supports $A,B$ given $L$. Their joint mass with $L$ is proportional to $1/N(L)$, so given $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$ the nuisance rows are not asserted uniform. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $\gamma_{-1}$ and let $C\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$ be the cross-block matrix with first row zero and remaining rows $\epsilon\gamma_l\lambda_l$. Under $Q_{\gamma_{-1},L}$, after canceling $s$, the covariance is $B_0=\begin{pmatrix}I_r&C\\C^{\mathsf T}&I_r\end{pmatrix}$, with an extra identity coordinate if $p$ is odd. Put $R=(I_r-C^{\mathsf T}C)^{1/2}$; it is positive definite because $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1$. The block matrix $T=\begin{pmatrix}I_r&0\\C^{\mathsf T}&R\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $TT^{\mathsf T}=B_0$. Whiten by $T^{-1}$, extended by the identity on any extra coordinate. If $e=e_1$ is the first coordinate in the left block and $v_A=\mathbf1_A$ is the right-block support vector, then $T^{-1}e=e$ and $T^{-1}v_A=R^{-1}v_A$. Thus the alternative covariances become $I+\Delta_A$ and $I+\Delta_B$, where $\Delta_A=eu^{\mathsf T}+ue^{\mathsf T}$, $\Delta_B=ew^{\mathsf T}+we^{\mathsf T}$, $u=\epsilon R^{-1}v_A$, $w=\epsilon R^{-1}v_B$, and $u,w\perp e$. With $H=(I_r-C^{\mathsf T}C)^{-1}$, $u^{\mathsf T}w=t=\epsilon^2\mathbf1_A^{\mathsf T}H\mathbf1_B$. The operator norms of $\Delta_A,\Delta_B$ equal $\|u\|_2,\|w\|_2$, respectively. Since $\|R^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)^{-1/2}$, these norms are at most $\epsilon\sqrt{k}/\sqrt{1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2}<1/4$ for large $P_0$; here $\epsilon\sqrt{k}=(k\epsilon)/\sqrt{k}\le C/(\sqrt2\log p)$. For positive-definite $S$, [F1], [F6] and [F7] give the Lebesgue density $f_S(x)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det S)^{-1/2}\exp(-x^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}x/2)$: the independent standard-normal coordinates have product density, and the invertible linear map $S^{1/2}$ changes variables with determinant $(\det S)^{1/2}$. For the one-observation laws, write $f_A,f_B,f_0$ for the positive densities of the two alternatives and the whitened baseline. Put $M=(I+\Delta_A)^{-1}+(I+\Delta_B)^{-1}-I$. Each inverse has smallest eigenvalue at least $(1+1/4)^{-1}=4/5$, hence $M\succeq(3/5)I$. The product density $f_Af_B/f_0$ has exponent matrix $M$ and normalizing factor $(2\pi)^{-p/2}[\det(I+\Delta_A)\det(I+\Delta_B)]^{-1/2}$. Diagonalizing $M$ by [F4], applying an orthogonal change of variables and scaling each one-dimensional standard-normal density [F6, F7] gives $$\int \frac{f_A(x)f_B(x)}{f_0(x)}\,dx=[\det(I+\Delta_A)\det(I+\Delta_B)\det M]^{-1/2}.$$ The identity $(I+\Delta_A)M(I+\Delta_B)=I-\Delta_A\Delta_B$ and determinant multiplicativity [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]] reduce it to $\det(I-\Delta_A\Delta_B)^{-1/2}$. Since $u,w\perp e$, $\Delta_A\Delta_B=tee^{\mathsf T}+uw^{\mathsf T}$. On $\operatorname{span}\{e\}$, $I-\Delta_A\Delta_B$ contributes determinant $1-t$. On $e^\perp$, if $u=0$ the rank-one determinant is $1$; otherwise choose an orthonormal basis whose first vector is $u/\|u\|_2$, so $I-uw^{\mathsf T}$ has only its first row changed and determinant $1-w^{\mathsf T}u=1-t$. The full determinant is $(1-t)^2$, and the one-observation cross integral is $(1-t)^{-1}$. The n-sample laws have product densities by the product joint-law supplier in [F6]; repeated Tonelli [F8] therefore makes their cross integral the nth power, $(1-t)^{-n}$. [given, F1, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Write $J=|A\cap B|$, $X_l=|A\cap\operatorname{supp}\lambda_l|$ and $Y_l=|B\cap\operatorname{supp}\lambda_l|$. The identity $H-I=C^{\mathsf T}(I-CC^{\mathsf T})^{-1}C$ follows from $H-I=(I-C^{\mathsf T}C)^{-1}C^{\mathsf T}C$ and $(I-C^{\mathsf T}C)C^{\mathsf T}=C^{\mathsf T}(I-CC^{\mathsf T})$. The Neumann series $(I-CC^{\mathsf T})^{-1}=\sum_{m\ge0}(CC^{\mathsf T})^m$ converges because $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1$; since $C$ has nonnegative entries, $H-I$ is entrywise nonnegative and $t-J\epsilon^2\ge0$. The eigenvalues of $CC^{\mathsf T}$ lie in $[0,\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2]$, so [F4] gives $\|(I-CC^{\mathsf T})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)^{-1}$. Also $(C\mathbf1_A)_l=\epsilon\gamma_lX_l$ and $(C\mathbf1_B)_l=\epsilon\gamma_lY_l$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F5] and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ yield $$0\le t-J\epsilon^2\le\frac{\epsilon^4}{2(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)}\sum_{l=2}^r(X_l^2+Y_l^2).$$ Since $\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)^{-1}$ and $\|\mathbf1_A\|_2=\|\mathbf1_B\|_2=\sqrt{k}$, [F5] also gives $t\le\epsilon^2k/(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)$. Since $k\ge2$ and $k\epsilon\le C/\log p$, $\epsilon^2k=(k\epsilon)^2/k=o(1)$, so $t=o(1)$. The derivative of $-\log(1-x)$ is at most $2$ for $0\le x\le t\le1/2$; since $1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\ge8/9$, the preceding bound gives $$(1-t)^{-n}\le(1-J\epsilon^2)^{-n}\exp\left\{\theta\sum_{l=2}^r(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\right\},\qquad\theta=2n\epsilon^4.$$ [given, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Fix $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$ and all nuisance rows except row $l$, and let $a_j$ be the sum in column $j$ over those fixed rows. A support $S$ for row $l$ is feasible exactly when $|S|=k$, $a_j+\mathbf1_{\{j\in S\}}\le2k$ for every column, and $a_j+\mathbf1_{\{j\in S\}}<2k$ for every $j\in A\cup B$ (so both first-row supports remain available). Thus before prior weighting row $l$ is uniform over the $k$-subsets of the fixed set $$V=\{j\in A\cup B:a_j\le2k-2\}\cup\{j\notin A\cup B:a_j\le2k-1\}.$$ At most $(r-2)k/(2k)\le r/2$ columns outside $A\cup B$ have $a_j=2k$, so deleting these and $A\cup B$ leaves at least $r/2-2k\ge r/4$ available columns; hence $d_0=|V|\ge r/4$. The first-row availability count is $d(L)=\#\{j:a_j+\mathbf1_{\{j\in S\}}<2k\}$; as $S$ varies, only columns outside $A\cup B$ with $a_j=2k-1$ can change this count, so its range has width at most $k\le2k$. Since $d(L)\ge r/2$ and $\binom{d+1}k/\binom dk=(d+1)/(d+1-k)$, the ratio of any two weights $1/N(L)$ is at most $\exp(Ck^2/r)\le2$ after increasing $P_0$. Thus the actual conditional density of the row support is at most twice the uniform-subset density on $V$. If $m=|A\cap V|$, singleton and ordered-pair inclusion probabilities give $E X_l=mk/d_0\le Ck^2/r$ and $E[X_l(X_l-1)]=m(m-1)k(k-1)/(d_0(d_0-1))\le Ck^4/r^2$. Hence $E X_l^2\le C(k^2/r+k^4/r^2)$; the same bound holds for $Y_l$ and under the weighted law with twice the constant. Since $\theta k^2=o(1)$, $e^z-1\le2z$ for $0\le z\le1$ yields $$E[\exp\{\theta(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\}\mid\text{all other rows},A,B,\gamma_{-1}]\le1+C\theta(k^2/r+k^4/r^2).$$ [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Put $f_l=\exp\{\theta(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\}$ and $B_0=1+C\theta(k^2/r+k^4/r^2)$. Every factor except $f_l$ is measurable when all rows except $l$ are fixed. Thus for any subset $S$ containing $l$, conditional expectation gives $$E[\prod_{j\in S}f_j\mid A,B,\gamma_{-1}]\le B_0 E[\prod_{j\in S\setminus\{l\}}f_j\mid A,B,\gamma_{-1}].$$ Iterating over the finitely many nuisance rows yields $$E[\exp\{\theta\sum_{l=2}^r(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\}\mid A,B,\gamma_{-1}]\le B_0^{r-1}\le\exp\{Cn\epsilon^4(k^2+k^4/r)\}=1+o(1)$$ uniformly in $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$. No row independence is used. [given, step 1.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Given $L$, $A,B$ are independent uniform $k$-subsets of a set of size $d\ge r/2$. Expanding $z^J=(1+(z-1))^J$ and using $$E\binom Jj=\binom kj\frac{(k)_j}{(d)_j}\le\frac{[k^2/(d-k+1)]^j}{j!}$$ gives $E[z^J\mid L]\le\exp\{k^2(z-1)/(d-k+1)\}$. Since $J\le k$ and $\epsilon^2k=o(1)$, $(1-J\epsilon^2)^{-n}\le\exp(2n\epsilon^2J)=p^{2v^2J}$. Define $\chi^2(\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L},Q_{\gamma_{-1},L})=\int(d\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L}/dQ_{\gamma_{-1},L}-1)^2\,dQ_{\gamma_{-1},L}$. Finite expansion of the mixture density gives $$1+\chi^2(\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L},Q_{\gamma_{-1},L})=E_{A,B\mid L,\gamma_{-1}}(1-t)^{-n}.$$ The posterior of $L$ given $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$ has weights proportional to $1/N(L)$; step 6.1 bounds the conditional remainder factor by $1+o(1)$ uniformly in $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$. Since $d-k+1\ge r/3$, the overlap generating-function bound is uniform in $L,\gamma_{-1}$ and yields $$E_{\gamma_{-1},L}[1+\chi^2(\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L},Q_{\gamma_{-1},L})]\le(1+o(1))\exp(Ck^2p^{2v^2}/r)=1+o(1),$$ using step 1.1. For each fixed $(\gamma_{-1},L)$, if $R=d\overline P/dQ$, then $E_Q(R-1)=0$, so the positive and negative parts of $R-1$ have equal integrals, and the event $\{R\ge1\}$ attains the supremum in [F9]; hence $\operatorname{TV}(\overline P,Q)=\tfrac12E_Q|R-1|$; [F10] bounds this by $\tfrac12\sqrt{\chi^2(\overline P,Q)}$. Finite Cauchy--Schwarz [F5] over the common prior weights on $(\gamma_{-1},L)$ bounds the average conditional total variation by $\tfrac12\sqrt{E_{\gamma_{-1},L}\chi^2}$, at most $1/2$ after increasing $P_0$. The same mixing weights are used under bit $i=0$ and bit $i=1$, so the full sample-law mixtures have total variation at most $1/2$ by the triangle inequality for the density integral. Their density affinity satisfies $$\int\min(dP_{i,0},dP_{i,1})=1-\operatorname{TV}(P_{i,0},P_{i,1})\ge1/2.$$ [given, F5, F9, F10, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 For parameters with $h$ different bits, apply their covariance difference to the vector that is one on the right block and zero elsewhere. Each changed bit contributes a distinct left-block coordinate of magnitude $s\epsilon k$, independently of support choices, so the squared output norm is at least $h(s\epsilon k)^2$ while the input squared norm is $r$. Hence $\|\Sigma_\theta-\Sigma_{\theta'}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\ge h(s\epsilon k)^2/r$. Given any measurable matrix estimator, choose a nearest finite covariance target with a fixed tie order. The finite distance comparisons are measurable: [F5] bounds the operator norm by the Frobenius norm, and its triangle inequality follows by applying the Euclidean triangle inequality to every unit vector, so distance to each fixed target is continuous. A wrong target decision forces squared estimation loss at least one quarter of the squared target separation. For each bit, the sum of its two conditional testing errors is at least the density affinity, since pointwise the test contributes at least the minimum of the two densities. By step 7.1, under the uniform prior each bit error probability is at least $1/4$, so the average number of bit errors is at least $r/4$. The maximal risk is at least the average risk and therefore at least $(s\epsilon k)^2/16$. Finally, $k\ge c/[4(s\epsilon)^q]$ implies this is at least $b c^2a^{1-q}$ for a positive constant depending only on the fixed parameters. [given, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

anchors.quote:
Let a dominated finite-dimensional parametric model be quadratic-mean
differentiable, with the supplied density family of [[def-qmd-path]], at an interior point $\theta_0\in\mathbb R^d$, with score
$s_{\theta_0}\in L^2(P_{\theta_0};\mathbb R^d)$. Then
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}=0$.

2.1 For each coordinate vector $e_j$, set $h=te_j$ with $t>0$ small enough that $\theta_0+te_j\in\Theta$. Divide the relation from step 1.1 by $t$ and let $t\downarrow0$ to obtain $\mathbb E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0,j}=0$. This holds for all $j=1,\ldots,d$, hence the score vector has mean zero. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

anchors.quote:
Fix $\tau>0$, $0\le q<1$ and $\beta>1$. Let $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$,
$p\ge n^\beta$ and $a=\log(p)/n\le1$. For iid observations from
$\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], use
[[alg-entrywise-thresholded-sample-covariance]] with
$\lambda=8192\tau\sqrt a$. There is $C=C(q,\tau)<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)}\mathbb E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\le C\{c^2a^{1-q}+a\}.$$
The estimator uses sample centering and divisor $n$, including unknown means;
no independence between coordinates is assumed. This is the unmodified
threshold estimator, not a clipped version.

1.1 Put $u=\log(8p^{10})\le13\log p$. Since $a\le1$, $192\tau(\sqrt{u/n}+u/n)\le192\tau(\sqrt{13}+13)\sqrt a<4096\tau\sqrt a=\lambda/2$. The failure bound in [F2] is $1/(4p^9)+1/(32p^{18})\le p^{-8}$. Thus an event $G$ has $P^{\otimes n}$-probability at least $1-p^{-8}$, and on it [F3] bounds squared loss by $C(q,\tau)(c^2a^{1-q}+a)$. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Write $U_{ij}=X_{ij}-EX_{ij}$. By [F1] and [F4], $E_{P^{\otimes n}}|U_{ij}|^8\le(2\tau)^4\,4!=384\tau^4$. Also, for unit $v$, $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v\le\int_0^\infty e^{-t/(2\tau)}dt=2\tau$; applying [F6] to centered coordinates gives $|\sigma_{jk}|\le2\tau$. The sample-centered diagonal obeys $0\le\widehat\sigma^*_{jj}\le n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}^2$. Applying [F7] to the two centered coordinate sample vectors gives $|\widehat\sigma^*_{jk}|^2\le\widehat\sigma^*_{jj}\widehat\sigma^*_{kk}$. Therefore $$E_{P^{\otimes n}}|\widehat\sigma^*_{jk}|^4\le\tfrac12 E_{P^{\otimes n}}[(\widehat\sigma^*_{jj})^4+(\widehat\sigma^*_{kk})^4]\le384\tau^4,$$ where the final inequality uses [F8] with $y_i=U_{ij}^2$ (and likewise for $k$). These bounds are independent of the unknown means. [given, F1, F4, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 By [F5], $E_{P^{\otimes n}}|\widehat\sigma_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}|^4\le8E_{P^{\otimes n}}(|\widehat\sigma^*_{jk}|^4+|\sigma_{jk}|^4)\le C\tau^4$. For any matrix $A$, [F7] gives $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\le\sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^2$ by applying finite Cauchy–Schwarz to each row against a unit vector; [F7] also gives $(\sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^2)^2\le p^2\sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^4$. Thus $E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^4\le C\tau^4p^4$. Applying [F6] to $\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$ and $\mathbf1_{G^c}$ and using step 1.1 gives $$E_{P^{\otimes n}}[\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2;G^c]\le C\tau^2p^2p^{-4}=C\tau^2p^{-2}.$$ Since $p\ge n^\beta$ implies $n\le p^{1/\beta}\le p$ and $1/p\le\log p$, we have $p^{-2}\le\log p/n=a$. Adding the good-event bound proves the claim uniformly over the class. [given, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

anchors.quote: 2.1 On that event, [A2] gives $M_n(\hat\theta_n)\le M(\theta_0)-\gamma+U_n$ and $M_n(\theta_0)\ge M(\theta_0)-U_n$. The approximate-maximization inequality [A4] also gives $M_n(\hat\theta_n)\ge M_n(\theta_0)-\rho_n$. Combining them yields $\gamma\le2U_n+\rho_n$. [A2, A3, A4, step 1.1, algebra]

Step 2.1 therefore gives $P^{\otimes n}\{d(\hat\theta_n,\theta_0)\ge\varepsilon\}\to0$, which implies the strict-error probability in [F3] tends to zero. Thus $\hat\theta_n$ is consistent. anchors.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law
$P_{\theta_0}$ in a dominated parametric model
$\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$, where $\Theta$ is open in $\mathbb R^d$,
$d\ge1$, and $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Let $p_\theta$ be densities with respect
to one supplied sigma-finite measure. Suppose the model is QMD at $\theta_0$
with score $s_{\theta_0}$ and positive-definite information
$I=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$. Assume there are a
neighborhood $V$ of $\theta_0$ and a nonnegative measurable $L$ with
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}L^2<\infty$ such that, on one $P_{\theta_0}$-full set,
$$
|\log p_{\theta_1}(x)-\log p_{\theta_2}(x)|\le L(x)\|\theta_1-\theta_2\| \qquad(\theta_1,\theta_2\in V).
$$
Suppose a measurable exact MLE $\hat\theta_n$ exists and is consistent, in
the sense that $P_{\theta_0}(\|\hat\theta_n-\theta_0\|>\varepsilon)\to0$
for every $\varepsilon>0$. Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=I^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n s_{\theta_0}(X_i)+o_{P_{\theta_0}}(1)\ \Rightarrow\ N_d(0,I^{-1}).$$
Under the same local hypotheses, every consistent measurable exact likelihood
maximizer over a possibly $n$-dependent subset that contains $\theta_0$ is
also root-$n$ bounded in probability.
The conclusion is asymptotic; it gives no exact finite-sample normal law.

2.1 Normalize the absolutely continuous part on $S_0$ by $q_t=p_{\theta_0+t}\mathbf1_{S_0}/(1-\alpha_t)$, and put $a_t=\sqrt{q_t/p_{\theta_0}}-1$ on $S_0$. Since $\alpha_t=o(\|t\|^2)$, [F3] gives $a_t=\tfrac12t^Ts_{\theta_0}+o_{L^2(P_0)}(\|t\|)$, so $\mathbb E_0a_t^2=\tfrac14t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2)$ and $2\mathbb E_0a_t+\mathbb E_0a_t^2=0$ from $\mathbb E_0(1+a_t)^2=1$. The local envelope makes $f_t=\log(p_{\theta_0+t}/p_{\theta_0})$ square-integrable on $S_0$ and $\|f_t\|_2=O(\|t\|)$. Along every sequence $t\to0$ with $t/\|t\|\to u$, the $L^2$ convergence of $a_t/\|t\|$ has an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence. On it, $2\log(1+a_t)/\|t\|\to u^Ts_{\theta_0}$ pointwise. Since $|f_t|/\|t\|\le L$ and $s_{\theta_0}\in L^2(P_0)$, $|f_t/\|t\|-u^Ts_{\theta_0}|^2\le2L^2+2\|s_{\theta_0}\|^2$; dominated convergence [F10] gives convergence in $L^2$ along that subsequence. Every subsequence has such a subsubsequence, so convergence holds for the full sequence. Sequential compactness of the unit sphere therefore yields $f_t=t^Ts_{\theta_0}+o_{L^2(P_0)}(\|t\|)$. Moreover, the squares $a_t^2/\|t\|^2$ are uniformly integrable because $a_t/\|t\|$ converges in $L^2$ along every convergent direction. Taking the logarithm expansion in expectation requires a tail check. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. On $|a_t|\le\varepsilon$, the Taylor remainder $2\log(1+a_t)-2a_t+a_t^2$ is bounded by $\omega(\varepsilon)a_t^2$, where $\omega(\varepsilon)\to0$. Uniform integrability gives $\mathbb E_0[a_t^2\mathbf1_{|a_t|>\varepsilon}] =o(\|t\|^2)$ and therefore $P_0(|a_t|>\varepsilon)=o(\|t\|^2)$. On this tail, $|2\log(1+a_t)|\le |f_t|+|\log(1-\alpha_t)|$; its expectation is $o(\|t\|^2)$ by the envelope, Cauchy–Schwarz [F9], and the tail probability. The tail expectations of $|a_t|$ and $a_t^2$ are also $o(\|t\|^2)$ by [F9] and uniform integrability. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves that the expected Taylor remainder is $o(\|t\|^2)$. Taking expectations then gives $\mathbb E_0 f_t=2\mathbb E_0a_t-\mathbb E_0a_t^2+o(\|t\|^2) =-\tfrac12t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2);$ the normalization term $\log(1-\alpha_t)$ is $o(\|t\|^2)$. [A2, A3, F2, F3, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The squared Hellinger distance $H^2(P_{\theta_0+t},P_0)=\int(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}})^2d\mu$ equals $\tfrac14t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2)$ by step 1.1. The affinity $\rho_t=\int\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}p_{\theta_0}}d\mu=1-H^2/2$. On $S_0$ let $Y=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}/p_{\theta_0}}$, so $\mathbb E_0Y=\rho_t$. For $y>0$, $\log y\le\log\rho_t+(y-\rho_t)/\rho_t$ follows from $z-1-\log z\ge0$ for $z=y/\rho_t$, since this function has derivative $1-1/z$ and its minimum is $0$ at $z=1$; integrating gives $P_0f_t=2\mathbb E_0\log Y\le2\log\rho_t$. Since $\log(1-x)\le-x$ for $0\le x<1$ because $-x-\log(1-x)$ has derivative $x/(1-x)\ge0$ and value $0$ at $x=0$. Thus $2\log\rho_t\le-H^2$, so for some $c,\delta>0$, $P_0f_t\le-c\|t\|^2$ whenever $\|t\|\le\delta_0$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\mathbb G_n f=\sqrt n(P_nf-P_0f)$ for the empirical measure $P_n$. The pointwise Lipschitz envelope gives $\|f_t-f_v\|_{L^2(P_0)}\le\|L\|_2\|t-v\|$. The sample and mean processes are continuous in $t$ on compact local balls, so their suprema equal suprema over countable dense subsets and are measurable. To bound the local supremum, take an independent ghost sample $X'_1,\ldots,X'_n$. For each fixed original sample, the supremum of absolute values is convex in the ghost sample vector, so Jensen's inequality replaces $P_0f$ by $n^{-1}\sum_i f(X'_i)$ in the expected supremum. Swapping each pair $(X_i,X'_i)$ with an independent sign and then using the triangle inequality bounds that supremum by twice the expected conditional Rademacher supremum. Condition on the observations for the latter. For the conditional Rademacher process $R_n(f)=n^{-1/2}\sum_i\epsilon_i f(X_i)$, Hoeffding's exponential bound $\mathbb E_\epsilon e^{\lambda(R_n(f)-R_n(g))}= \prod_i\cosh(\lambda(f-g)(X_i)/\sqrt n)\le \exp\{\lambda^2P_n(f-g)^2/2\}$, since $\log\cosh u\le u^2/2$ (integrate $\tanh u\le u$ for $u\ge0$ and use evenness), makes each increment sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $P_n(f-g)^2\le P_nL^2\|t-v\|^2$. Choose successively finer dyadic Euclidean nets of the radius-$r$ parameter ball. At level $k$ the net has at most $(C2^k)^d$ points, each increment from its level-$(k-1)$ parent has scale at most $Cr2^{-k}(P_nL^2)^{1/2}$, and the expected maximum of $N$ centered sub-Gaussian variables of scale $\sigma$ is at most $\sigma\sqrt{2\log(2N)}$, by the exponential-moment bound and optimizing $\lambda$. Summing the resulting bounds uses the convergent series $\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}\sqrt{k}$ and gives $\mathbb E_\epsilon\sup_{\|t\|\le r}|R_n(f_t-f_0)|\le C_dr(P_nL^2)^{1/2}$. Symmetrization and $\mathbb E(P_nL^2)^{1/2}\le(P_0L^2)^{1/2}$ therefore give $\mathbb E\sup_{\|t\|\le r}|\mathbb G_n(f_t-f_0)|\le C_d r\|L\|_2.$ For $r_t=f_t-t^Ts_{\theta_0}$, step 2.1 gives $\sup_{\|t\|\le M/\sqrt n}P_0r_t^2=o(n^{-1})$, and increments have the square-integrable pointwise envelope $L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|$. Fix a mesh $\varepsilon>0$ and cover the bounded $h$-ball by finitely many mesh-$\varepsilon$ points. At each center $h_j$, the variance of $\sqrt n\mathbb G_nr_{h_j/\sqrt n}$ is $n\operatorname{Var}_0(r_{h_j/\sqrt n})\le nP_0r_{h_j/\sqrt n}^2=o(1)$, so Chebyshev and finiteness of the net make the maximum over centers $o_P(1)$. For increments within cells, form $g_h=r_{h/\sqrt n}-r_{h_j/\sqrt n}$, where $h_j$ is the center of the cell containing $h$. Each $g_h$ is pointwise bounded by $\varepsilon(L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|)/\sqrt n$. Apply conditional Rademacher chaining to the union of cell classes: at dyadic level $k$ there are at most $C_M\varepsilon^{-d}2^{kd}$ links, each with conditional scale at most $C\varepsilon2^{-k}(P_n(L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|)^2)^{1/2}$ after the $\sqrt n$ normalization. The exponential maximum bound and summation of $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k}\sqrt{\log(C_M\varepsilon^{-d})+C_dk}$ give an expected supremum at most $C_M\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(C_M/\varepsilon)}$ after symmetrization and $\mathbb E(P_n(L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|)^2)^{1/2}\le \|L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|\|_2$. Markov's inequality then shows that these cell increments vanish in probability as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves $\sup_{\|h\|\le M}|\sqrt n\mathbb G_nr_{h/\sqrt n}|=o_P(1)$. Thus, for each fixed $M$, uniformly over $\|h\|\le M$, $$\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_{P_0}(1),\qquad\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns_{\theta_0}(X_i).$$ The expectation term is step 2.1; the centered term follows by writing $f_t=t^Ts_{\theta_0}+(f_t-t^Ts_{\theta_0})$ and using the two net bounds. [A3, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Reduce $\delta_0$ if needed so the log envelope holds on the radius $2\delta_0$ ball, and put $\delta=\delta_0/2$. Consistency makes $\hat\theta_n$ lie within $\delta$ of $\theta_0$ with probability tending to one. On the dyadic shells $r_j\le\|t\|\le2r_j$ with $r_j=2^jM/\sqrt n$, exact maximization and $\ell_n(\hat\theta_n)\ge\ell_n(\theta_0)$ require $\sqrt n\sup_{\|t\|\le2r_j}|\mathbb G_nf_t|\ge c n r_j^2$. The expectation bound in step 3.1 and Markov's inequality [F11] bound the probability of this event by $C/(\sqrt n r_j)=C/(2^jM)$. Summing the geometric series and then letting $M\to\infty$ proves $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=O_{P_0}(1)$ using [F4]. The argument used only consistency, feasibility of $\theta_0$, and the maximizing inequality; it therefore proves the same bound for any exact maximizer over a subset containing $\theta_0$. [A3, F4, F11, step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra]

5.1 Put $\hat h_n=\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ and $h_n^*=I^{-1}\Delta_n$. The multivariate CLT [F7] and [F5] make $h_n^*=O_{P_0}(1)$; step 4.1 makes $\hat h_n=O_{P_0}(1)$. For $Q_n(h)=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh$, $Q_n(h_n^*)-Q_n(h)=\tfrac12(h-h_n^*)^TI(h-h_n^*) \ge\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(I)\|h-h_n^*\|^2.$ Uniform convergence on bounded balls in step 3.1, feasibility of bounded local $h$ because $\theta_0$ is interior, and exact MLE maximization therefore force $\hat h_n-h_n^*=o_{P_0}(1)$. [A3, F4, F5, F7, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The CLT [F7] gives $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,I)$; the limiting law exists by [F8]. Since $I$ is invertible, $h_n^*=I^{-1}\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,I^{-1})$ by the continuous linear map. Combining this with step 5.1 by [F6] proves both the asymptotic linear representation and the stated normal limit. AC is used only through [F7]–[F8]. [A1, A2, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 5.1] ∎

anchors.quote:
Assume AC. Fix $\beta>1$, $M,\tau>0$, and $0\le q<1$. For all integers
$n\ge1$, $p\ge2$ with $p\ge n^\beta$, and every radius
$$0\le c=c_{n,p}\le M n^{(1-q)/2}(\log p)^{-(3-q)/2},$$
put $a=\log(p)/n$ and $r_{n,p}=c^2a^{1-q}+a$. Over the law class
$\mathcal P_q(\tau,c)$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], the
minimax squared operator risk of [[def-minimax-squared-operator-risk]] satisfies
$$C_1\min\{1,r_{n,p}\}\le\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P_q(\tau,c))\le C_2\min\{1,r_{n,p}\},$$
where $0<C_1\le C_2<\infty$ depend only on $\beta,M,\tau,q$.
For $a\le1$, the unmodified estimator of
[[alg-entrywise-thresholded-sample-covariance]], with
$\lambda=8192\tau\sqrt a$, has expected squared operator risk at most
$C(q,\tau)r_{n,p}$. A rule attaining the capped upper bound in every
dimension is explicit: use that estimator when $r_{n,p}<1$, and output
the zero matrix when $r_{n,p}\ge1$. All original dimension regimes,
including super-exponential $p$, are retained; the risk saturates instead
of diverging. The raw threshold estimator alone is not claimed to attain
the cap outside its stated regime.

1.1 For any unit vector $v$, put $Y=v^{\mathsf T}(X-EX)$. By [F4] and layer cake [F6], $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v=E[Y^2]=\int_0^\infty P(Y^2>u)\,du\le\int_0^\infty e^{-u/(2\tau)}\,du=2\tau$. By [F5], $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, so [F7] gives $\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\tau$. The constant zero estimator therefore has squared loss at most $4\tau^2$. If $r_{n,p}\ge1$, this proves the capped upper bound for the specified switch. If $r_{n,p}<1$, then $a<1$, and [F1] proves it for the threshold branch. The switch is measurable, since its branch depends only on the known dimensions and class radius; the threshold operations are measurable entrywise. [given, F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

1.2 Let $P_0$ and $v$ be the fixed constants in [F3]. For $p<P_0$, $n\le p^{1/\beta}<P_0^{1/\beta}$, so $a\ge\log2/P_0^{1/\beta}$. Thus [F2] is bounded below by a positive fixed-parameter constant, which dominates a constant multiple of $\min\{1,r_{n,p}\}\le1$. For $a\ge1$, [F2] likewise gives this constant lower bound, regardless of $p$. These arguments cover all finite-size and saturated-dimension cases without a hidden asymptotic restriction. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 It remains to consider $p\ge P_0$ and $a<1$. If $c/[2(sv\sqrt a)^q]<2$, then $c^2a^{1-q}<16(sv)^{2q}a$, and [F2] alone bounds the risk below by a positive fixed-parameter multiple of $r_{n,p}$; this includes all effective sparse counts rounding to zero and $q=0$. Otherwise [F3] supplies the sparse term, while [F2] supplies the $a$ term. The maximum of two nonnegative lower bounds is at least half their sum, giving a fixed-parameter multiple of $r_{n,p}$ and hence of its cap. Combining with step 1.2 and the upper bound proves the result. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid from $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], with $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$, and $\tau>0$. Let $u>0$ and let $\widehat\Sigma^\ast$ be the sample-centered covariance. Then
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le j,k\le p}|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}| \le192\tau\left(\sqrt{\frac un}+\frac un\right)\right)\ge1-2pe^{-u}-2p^2e^{-2u}.$$
In particular $u=\log(8p^4)$ gives the original probability $1-p^{-2}$.
No independence between coordinates of a single observation is assumed.

1.1 Put $U_i=X_i-\mu$. For coordinate unit vectors $e_j,e_k$, [F1] gives the required tail bounds for $U_{ij}$ and $U_{ik}$. Hence [F2] makes $W_i^{jk}=U_{ij}U_{ik}-\sigma_{jk}$ centered sub-exponential with parameters $(1024\tau^2,16\tau)$. For fixed $(j,k)$ these variables are independent across $i$ by [F6]. [F1, F2, F6, F8, given]

1.2 By [F4], each $U_{ij}$ is sub-Gaussian with proxy $64\tau$. Independence across $i$ and [F7] give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}}\le\prod_i e^{32\tau\lambda^2/n^2}=e^{32\tau\lambda^2/n},$ so each $\bar U_j=n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}$ has proxy $64\tau/n$. Apply [F5] at $s=\sqrt{128\tau u/n}$ to obtain $\mathbb P\!\left(\max_j|\bar U_j|>s\right)\le2p e^{-u}.$ [F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 Set $r=u/n$ and $t=64\tau(\sqrt r+r)$. Applying [F3] to $n^{-1}\sum_iW_i^{jk}$ gives $\mathbb P\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_iW_i^{jk}\right|>t\right)\le2\exp\!\left[-\frac12\min\!\left\{\frac{nt^2}{1024\tau^2},\frac{nt}{16\tau}\right\}\right]\le2e^{-2u},$ because each expression inside the minimum is at least $4u$. A union bound over $p^2$ ordered pairs gives failure probability at most $2p^2e^{-2u}$. [F3, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Expanding [F8] gives $\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}=n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}U_{ik}-\bar U_j\bar U_k$. On the intersection of the mean event in step 1.2 and the entrywise event in step 2.1, $|\bar U_j\bar U_k|\le(\bar U_j^2+\bar U_k^2)/2\le s^2$, so every entry error is at most $64\tau(\sqrt r+r)+128\tau r\le192\tau(\sqrt r+r).$ The two failure probabilities sum to at most $2pe^{-u}+2p^2e^{-2u}$ by [F9]. At $u=\log(8p^4)$ this is at most $p^{-2}$, proving the original specialization as well. [F8, F9, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

anchors.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC), as required by the library's multivariate iid central limit theorem. Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid $\mathcal X$-valued observations with law $P$. Let $\psi:\Theta\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly measurable and satisfy $P\|\psi_\theta\|<\infty$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$; write $\psi_\theta(x)=\psi(\theta,x)$. Let $\hat\theta_n:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\Theta,\mathcal B(\Theta))$ be a measurable estimator sequence as in [[def-estimator-sequence-in-iid-experiments]] and a Z-estimator as in [[def-z-estimator]], with the stronger root-rate condition below. Write
$$P\psi_\theta=\mathbb E[\psi_\theta(X_1)],\qquad P_n\psi_\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_\theta(X_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n\psi_\theta=\sqrt n(P_n-P)\psi_\theta.$$
Assume the displayed random vectors and suprema below are measurable, and suppose:

1. $\|\hat\theta_n-\theta_0\|=o_P(1)$ and $\sqrt n\,\|P_n\psi_{\hat\theta_n}\|=o_P(1)$.
2. $P\psi_{\theta_0}=0$, $P\|\psi_{\theta_0}\|^2<\infty$, and $\Sigma=P[\psi_{\theta_0}\psi_{\theta_0}^{T}]$.
3. The mean map $\Psi(\theta)=P\psi_\theta$ has expansion $\Psi(\theta_0+h)=Vh+\rho(h)$ with $V$ nonsingular and $\|\rho(h)\|/\|h\|\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$.
4. The local stochastic-equicontinuity condition holds: for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P^n\!\left(\sup_{\theta\in\Theta:\,\|\theta-\theta_0\|<\delta}\|\mathbb G_n(\psi_\theta-\psi_{\theta_0})\|>\varepsilon\right)=0.$$

Here $P^n$ denotes the product sampling law of $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$.

Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=-V^{-1}\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1)\Rightarrow N_d(0,V^{-1}\Sigma V^{-T}).$$
This theorem assumes consistency and the local empirical-process condition; it asserts neither. The local equicontinuity condition is the direct process hypothesis used in the proof, and consistency alone does not replace it.

1.1 Fix $\varepsilon,\eta>0$. By [A2] choose $\delta>0$ such that the limiting upper probability of the displayed supremum exceeding $\varepsilon$ is at most $\eta$. By [A1], $P^n(\|\hat\theta_n-\theta_0\|\ge\delta)\to0$. On the complementary event, $\|\mathbb G_n(\psi_{\hat\theta_n}-\psi_{\theta_0})\|$ is bounded by that supremum. Hence its limiting upper tail probability is at most $\eta$; letting $\eta\downarrow0$ proves $\mathbb G_n(\psi_{\hat\theta_n}-\psi_{\theta_0})=o_P(1)$. [A1, A2, choose]

1.2 By [F12], applying the same measurable map $\psi_{\theta_0}$ to the iid observations preserves independence; identical distribution follows because every $X_i$ has the same law. By [A4] and [F5], $\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_{\theta_0}(X_i)$ is a centered iid sum with finite covariance $\Sigma$. AC is available by [F9], so [F7] gives $\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma)$, where convergence in distribution is weak convergence of laws by [F4]. In particular $\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}=O_P(1)$ by [F2]. [A4, F2, F4, F5, F7, F9, F12]

2.1 Put $h_n=\hat\theta_n-\theta_0$ and $W_n=\sqrt n\,h_n$. By [F10]–[F11], the estimator and root have the stated Z-estimator and data-measurability conventions; [A1] imposes the stronger root-rate residual, which is also $o_P(1)$ since $n^{-1/2}\le1$. The identity $\sqrt nP_n\psi_{\hat\theta_n}=\mathbb G_n\psi_{\hat\theta_n}+\sqrt n\Psi(\hat\theta_n)$, [A1], step 1.1 and the derivative expansion in [A3], as specified by [F6], give $VW_n+\sqrt n\,\rho(h_n)=-\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1)$. Moreover $\|\rho(h_n)\|/\|h_n\|=o_P(1)$ by [A1] and [A3], with the ratio set to zero when $h_n=0$. [A1, A3, F6, F10, F11, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $V$ is nonsingular, [A3] and step 2.1 imply $\|W_n\|\le\|V^{-1}\|(\|\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}\|+e_n+a_n\|W_n\|)$, where $e_n=o_P(1)$ and $a_n=\|\rho(h_n)\|/\|h_n\|=o_P(1)$ (set $a_n=0$ if $h_n=0$). With probability tending to one, $\|V^{-1}\|a_n\le1/2$. Absorbing that term and using $\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}=O_P(1)$ from step 1.2 proves $W_n=O_P(1)$. [A3, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Now $\sqrt n\,\rho(h_n)=o_P(1)$ because it is the product of $\|W_n\|=O_P(1)$ and $\|\rho(h_n)\|/\|h_n\|=o_P(1)$. Substituting into step 2.1 gives $W_n=-V^{-1}\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1)$. [A3, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By [F4], [F7], and [F8], the continuous linear image $-V^{-1}\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}$ converges to a centered Gaussian with covariance $V^{-1}\Sigma V^{-T}$: for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$, the projection of $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ along $-V^{-T}u$ is centered normal with variance $u^TV^{-1}\Sigma V^{-T}u$. Applying [F3] to the $o_P(1)$ remainder in step 4.1 proves the asserted normal limit. AC is used in the multivariate iid CLT and the normal-law supplier, not in the stochastic-order or Taylor steps. [F3, F4, F7, F8, F9, step 1.2, step 4.1] ∎

anchors.quote: 1.1 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. If $\{\theta:d(\theta,\theta_0)\ge\varepsilon\}$ is empty, the corresponding metric-error event is empty and its probability is zero for every $n$. Otherwise $b=b_\varepsilon$ is finite and positive: [A3] gives positivity, and any point in this nonempty set has a finite population equation norm by integrability in [A1]. Put $V_n=\sup_\theta\|\Psi_n(\theta)-\Psi(\theta)\|$ and $R_n=\|\Psi_n(\hat\theta_n)\|$. Both are measurable, and $V_n=o_P(1)$ and $R_n=o_P(1)$ by [A2] and [A4]. The remaining steps treat this nonempty case. [A1, A2, A3, A4, F2, choose, F1]

2.1 On the event $d(\hat\theta_n,\theta_0)\ge\varepsilon$, separation and the triangle inequality give $$b\le\|\Psi(\hat\theta_n)\|\le\|\Psi(\hat\theta_n)-\Psi_n(\hat\theta_n)\|+\|\Psi_n(\hat\theta_n)\|\le V_n+R_n.$$ Thus the metric-error event is contained in $\{V_n+R_n\ge b\}$. This uses the equation error itself, with no representation of the nonlinear quantity $-\|P_n\psi_\theta\|$ as an empirical average of a fixed criterion. [A1, A3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $b>0$, the union bound gives $P^{\otimes n}(V_n+R_n\ge b)\le P^{\otimes n}(V_n>b/3)+P^{\otimes n}(R_n>b/3)\to0$ by [F2] and step 1.1. Step 2.1 therefore implies $P^{\otimes n}\{d(\hat\theta_n,\theta_0)\ge\varepsilon\}\to0$, and hence the same holds with strict inequality. Together with the empty case of step 1.1, this proves consistency for every $\varepsilon>0$ by [F4]. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, given] ∎

cex-local-linear-finite-sample-expectati.exact_claim_quote:
At a fixed one-dimensional interior point, suppose the design density is
positive and $C^2$ locally, the chosen regression function is $C^2$ locally,
and the conditional response variance is finite and continuous. Suppose
$K$ is nonnegative, symmetric, positive near zero, normalized, with finite
positive second moment and finite squared integral. If $h_n\to0$,
$nh_n\to\infty$ and $nh_n^3\to\infty$, then the empirical local-linear fit
with a fixed fallback only on singular designs has a Lebesgue expectation

def-local-polynomial-estimator.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix $n\ge1$, a point
$x\in\mathbb R$, bandwidth $h>0$, degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K$, and fallback $a_0\in\mathbb R$. Set
$u_i=(x-X_i)/h$, $r_p(u)=(1,u,\ldots,u^p)^\mathsf T$, let $Z$ be the matrix
whose $i$th row is $r_p(u_i)^\mathsf T$, let
$W=\operatorname{diag}(K(u_1),\ldots,K(u_n))$, and put
$M=Z^\mathsf TWZ$. If $M$ is nonsingular, define
$$\widehat\beta=M^{-1}Z^\mathsf TW(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^\mathsf T,\qquad \widehat m_{p,h}(x)=\widehat\beta_0.$$
If $M$ is singular, define $\widehat m_{p,h}(x)=a_0$. For fixed $x,h,n,p$
and Borel $K$, this is a real statistic estimating the pointwise target
$m(x)$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The case $p=1$ is the
**local-linear estimator**. No claim that $M$ is nonsingular for a given
sample is implicit in this definition.

def-nadaraya-watson-estimator.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$,
a prediction point $x\in\mathbb R$, a bandwidth $h>0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$, and a fixed fallback
$a_0\in\mathbb R$. For data $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$, put
$$D_{n,h}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h).$$
The **Nadaraya–Watson estimator** of the pointwise target $m(x)$ is
$$\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h}(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h)Y_i}{D_{n,h}(x)},&D_{n,h}(x)>0,\\[6pt] a_0,&D_{n,h}(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
For fixed $x,h,n$, this is a statistic of the observed sample with real target
$m(x)$, in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The fallback is part
of the definition. Kernel regularity and bandwidth assumptions used for bias
or variance results are stated in those results.

def-pointwise-regression-risk.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC as used to select the regression version. Fix a statistical experiment indexed by $\theta$, a point $x$, a real
regression target $m_\theta(x)$, and a real-valued estimator
$T_x$ of that target, meaning a measurable statistic with target space
$\mathbb R$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. At this point, use the
squared-error loss
$$L_x(\theta,a)=(a-m_\theta(x))^2,\qquad a\in\mathbb R.$$
Its **pointwise squared-error risk** is the possibly infinite quantity
$$R_x(\theta,T_x)=\int (T_x(z)-m_\theta(x))^2\,P_\theta(dz)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the deterministic-rule specialization of the risk in
[[def-loss-function-and-risk]]: the action space is $\mathbb R$ with its
Borel sigma-algebra, the action is $T_x(z)$, and the loss section is
measurable because it is continuous in $a$. The integral is nonnegative, so
it is defined without a finite-moment assumption.

def-regression-target-version.exact_claim_quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real random variables on a probability
space, with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, and choose a regular conditional law
$Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$. On
$D=\{x:\int |y|\,Q(x,dy)<\infty\}$ define
$m(x)=\int y\,Q(x,dy)$, and put $m(x)=0$ off $D$. By
[[cor-conditional-expectation-as-a-measurable-function-of-the-conditioning-variable]],
$m$ is Borel measurable and $m(X)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(X)]$. A **regression target** is the resulting
$P_X$-almost-sure equivalence class; a **chosen regression-function version**
is the particular Borel function selected by the specified conditional law.

Pointwise smoothness is an additional hypothesis on the chosen version. It is
not implied by existence of conditional expectation, and statements about
$m(x)$ at a specified point use that selected version.

ex-local-linear-reproduces-affine-regres.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Let $X,Y$ be real random
variables with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$ and $Y=a+bX$ almost surely. Choose the
regular conditional law $Q(t,dy)=\delta_{a+bt}(dy)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$;
then the chosen regression-function version is $m(t)=a+bt$ at every point.
For any observed sample and any $x,h$ whose degree-one local moment matrix is
nonsingular, the local-linear estimate equals $a+bx$, even when the design
points are asymmetric around $x$.

lem-local-linear-normalized-moment-matri.exact_claim_quote:
Let $X_i$ be iid real random variables with density $f$ continuous and
positive at a fixed point $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative,
symmetric, with $\int K=1$ and $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, a globally bounded density $f$, or a bounded
rapid-tail kernel satisfying $\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$.
For $h=h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, set $U_i=(x-X_i)/h_n$ and
$$M_n=\frac1{nh_n}\sum_{i=1}^nK(U_i)\begin{pmatrix}1\\U_i\end{pmatrix}(1,U_i).$$
Then
$$M_n\longrightarrow f(x)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu_2\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{in probability},$$
and $\mathbb P(M_n\text{ is nonsingular})\to1$.
More generally, the proof establishes $(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_i L(U_i)\to f(x)\int L$
for any integrable Borel function $L$, if $f$ is bounded globally or $L$
has compact support. Boundedness or square integrability of $L$ is unnecessary.

thm-kernel-regression-conditional-asympt.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC for the chosen regression version. Let $X_i$ be independent and
identically distributed with density $f$ continuous and positive at an
interior point $x$. For the chosen conditional law $Q(t,dy)$ in
[[def-regression-target-version]], set
$\sigma^2(t)=\int (y-m(t))^2Q(t,dy)$ where finite. Conditional on the
predictor vector, assume the responses are independent, have means $m(X_i)$,
and have variances $\sigma^2(X_i)$, where $\sigma^2$ is finite and continuous
at $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative, symmetric, with $\int K=1$,
$0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$ and $R(K)=\int K^2<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, globally bounded $f,\sigma^2$, or the
rapid-tail alternative: $\mathbb E Y^2<\infty$, bounded $K$, and
$\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$. In this last alternative the stated
local continuity is sufficient.
For the local-linear conclusion also assume $\int u^2K(u)^2\,du<\infty$;
this extra squared moment is automatic for compactly supported kernels.
The Nadaraya–Watson conclusion requires only $R(K)<\infty$. For $h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, use the fixed
fallbacks in [[def-nadaraya-watson-estimator]] and
[[def-local-polynomial-estimator]]. Then, with variance taken conditionally
on $X_1,\ldots,X_n$,
$$nh_n\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x)\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n) \longrightarrow \frac{R(K)\sigma^2(x)}{f(x)} \quad\text{in probability},$$
and the same limit holds with $\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x)$ replaced by
the degree-one local-linear estimator. This is a conditional-variance
statement for both estimators. If additionally $m$ is continuous at $x$
and bounded globally (only bounded near $x$ is required for compact $K$),
or if the rapid-tail alternative holds and $m$ is continuous at $x$,
with $nh_n^3\to\infty$ additionally in this rapid-tail unconditional clause,
then the Nadaraya–Watson estimator is square-integrable for large $n$ and
$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x))=\frac{R(K)\sigma^2(x)}{nh_nf(x)}+o((nh_n)^{-1}).$$
No unconditional local-linear variance is asserted: near-singular designs
can make even its finite-sample expectation undefined.

thm-local-linear-conditional-bias.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC for the chosen regression version. Let $X_i$ be iid with density
$f$, with $f(x)>0$ at a fixed interior point $x$, and let $f,m$ be $C^2$
near $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative and symmetric, with
$\int K=1$, $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K<\infty$ and
$\int(1+u^2)K(u)^2\,du<\infty$. Assume either compact kernel support, or
that $f,m$ and their first two derivatives are bounded and continuous
globally. A further localization alternative, including the Gaussian kernel, is that
$\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$, $K$ is bounded, and
$$\lim_{A\to\infty}\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)=0.$$
Under this rapid-tail alternative only the stated local smoothness of
$f,m$ is needed; no global boundedness of $m$ or of its derivatives is assumed.
Let $h_n\to0$ with $nh_n^3\to\infty$. For almost every realized design,
integrate the degree-one fit of [[def-local-polynomial-estimator]] against
the independent response laws $\prod_iQ(X_i,dy_i)$; call the resulting
finite response-law mean $b_n(x)$, with the same fixed fallback on singular
designs. Then
$$b_n(x)-m(x)=\frac{h_n^2\mu_2}{2}m''(x)+o_P(h_n^2).$$
Here $Z_n=o_P(h_n^2)$ means $Z_n/h_n^2\to0$ in probability. This is a
conditional response-law mean statement; it neither assumes nor asserts
that the estimator has an unconditional Lebesgue expectation.

thm-local-linear-population-bias.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC for the chosen regression version [[def-regression-target-version]].
Let $X$ have density $f$, with $f(x)>0$ at a fixed interior point $x$,
and let $f,m$ be $C^2$ near $x$. Let $K$ be a finite-valued Borel,
nonnegative symmetric kernel with $\int K=1$,
$0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$ and $\int K^2<\infty$.
Assume either compact kernel support, or that $f,m$ and their first two
derivatives are bounded and continuous on $\mathbb R$.
A further localization alternative, including the Gaussian kernel, is that
$\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$, $K$ is bounded, and
$$\lim_{A\to\infty}\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)=0.$$
Under this rapid-tail alternative only the stated local smoothness of
$f,m$ is needed; no global boundedness of $m$ or of its derivatives is assumed.
Set
$$S_j(h)=\int K(u)u^j f(x-hu)\,du,\qquad T_j(h)=\int K(u)u^j f(x-hu)m(x-hu)\,du.$$
For sufficiently small $h$, $D_h=S_0S_2-S_1^2>0$ and the population
local-linear intercept, in the coordinates of [[def-local-polynomial-estimator]], is
$$m_{\mathrm{LL},h}(x)=\frac{S_2T_0-S_1T_1}{D_h}.$$
Then
$$m_{\mathrm{LL},h}(x)-m(x)=\frac{h^2\mu_2}{2}m''(x)+o(h^2).$$
This requires no fourth kernel moment.

thm-nadaraya-watson-finite-sample-bias.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC for the chosen regression version. Let $X_i$ be iid with density
$f$, and, conditional on the predictors, let the responses be independent
with the selected conditional laws $Q(X_i,dy)$, means $m(X_i)$ and variances

$\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$, $K$ is bounded, and

thm-nadaraya-watson-population-bias.exact_claim_quote:
Assume AC for the chosen regression version [[def-regression-target-version]].
Let $X$ have Lebesgue density $f$, with $f(x)>0$ at a fixed interior point
$x$, and let $f,m$ be $C^2$ near $x$. Let $K$ be a finite-valued Borel,
nonnegative, symmetric kernel with $\int K=1$,
$0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$ and $\int K^2<\infty$.

or boundedness of $K$ is required. The global alternative supplies tail
control for noncompact kernels; local smoothness alone does not supply it.
